path: 023. A storage schema changes only by recorded migration

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Create-only startup (status quo) R1 by construction: it cannot move existing data. R2: two databases dropped and recreated at different times have no guaranteed relationship. A mechanism for first runs, mistaken for a mechanism for change. Hand-run SQL per environment R2: environments drift the first time one is patched and another is not. R3: position lives in that person's memory. R4: statements run against a live database cannot be reviewed after. Treat every database as disposable Honest, and true of the current deployment. R1 the moment data is worth keeping. R5: "drop and recreate" is not a way of moving with a concept — it is a way of losing what the concept accumulated. Do nothing (keep dormant tooling) The wiring suggests the decision was made when it was not; an unused tool is not an arrangement. Every requirement is left to the next incident.
path: 023. A storage schema changes only by recorded migration

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 023. A storage schema changes only by recorded migration

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• A release carries a complete answer to "what happens to the data" (R1, R5).
  • Environments are comparable because they share one path (R2, R3).
  • Schema change becomes reviewable work, not an operational surprise (R4).
path: 023. A storage schema changes only by recorded migration

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• Every storage change gains a step it does not pay today, and in a system whose databases are all disposable that step is pure overhead until a real database exists.
  • Migrations are ordered, so parallel changes must reconcile with each other — a cost the create-only approach never charges.
  • The team operates a migration mechanism, including testing it, which the startup routine got for free.
path: 023. A storage schema changes only by recorded migration

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• The dormant tooling is evidence of intent, not of a decision: activating it, or replacing it with a mechanism that fits the stacks actually in use, is this record's first act on acceptance.
  • Drop-and-recreate stays legitimate for throwaway development databases and must be named as the exception wherever documented — visibly the exception, not the mechanism.
  • Backfills, dual writes, the period where two shapes coexist: change-management questions this record makes possible but does not answer.
  • The schema this record protects is what the retention rule (025) and recovery rule (026) later land on — a recorded migration path is a precondition for both.
Why is this Proposed and not Accepted?

The decision is that schema change becomes a recorded artifact; the mechanism that makes it true — the migration tool, its convention, the startup check — does not exist yet. Accepting now would record an intent no change can honour; the record is accepted in the pull request that lands the mechanism, where the claims become testable.
path: 023. A storage schema changes only by recorded migration

items.title: 024. A validated release is promoted by a declared path
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-07
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

A release is validated once and then moves by promotion: an environment receives the identical artifact, never a rebuilt one. The record's sharp edge is its scope. The system names and operates two environments, development and test, and hands every further environment a complete artifact rather than operating the promotion into it.
path: 024. A validated release is promoted by a declared path

items.title: Decision
items.text:
The system names the environments it operates: development, one person's machine, and test, the pipeline. A change becomes a release candidate by passing test. What happens to a released version after that is the adopting deployment's decision: acceptance and production exist only as customer- or project-specific arrangements, stated here rather than left to oral tradition.

The obligation to the rest is a complete hand-over: an artifact ready to promote — signed, versioned, and configured only by the settings an environment supplies. Where a deployment wants promotion to be a declared, repeatable path with a one-move rollback, it writes that path against the released artifact; the system neither operates it nor invents one on the deployment's behalf.

Both named environments run today. Development is the versioned container the whole system runs in; test is the pipeline that validates every change against real services. The decision is the boundary between what the system operates and what it hands over — and the mechanisms for the named environments already exist, which is why this record is Accepted rather than Proposed.
path: 024. A validated release is promoted by a declared path

items.title: Context
items.text:
The system releases as one versioned whole, and a release produces a complete set of deployable artifacts, validated together and signed so their origin is provable (029). Two environments are the system's own: development, where the whole system runs on one machine, and test, where the pipeline validates every change before it can become a release. Beyond test the picture changes shape — acceptance and production are where a customer's or project's requirements live, and they are not the same arrangement twice. The one part whose runtime is a cloud provider's reaches neither named environment today: it runs only in a local emulator, so its first real deployment will be unexercised.

This is not an accident of laziness; it is the honest shape of a system meant to be adopted rather than operated by the people who build it.

The boundary still has to be drawn. A reader who finds no statement will assume the missing environments are an oversight and build on them; a reader who finds a promotion path in the documentation will assume the system operates one. The cost of the ambiguity is paid at the worst moment: the first deployment that matters, by the person with the least room for error.

The question this record answers is what happens to a released version after it is published: which environments exist, what moving a version into one means, and who or what performs the move.
path: 024. A validated release is promoted by a declared path

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

  • R1 — The set of environments is stated. Where the system runs is written down, including which environments the system operates and which it hands over; "where does version N run?" has an answer that is not a question back.
  • R2 — Promotion is repeatable where the system operates. Moving a version into an environment the system runs is one declared action that produces the same result every time, performable by whoever is allowed to perform it, not only by whoever invented it.
  • R3 — The artifact does not change. What is promoted is the released, signed artifact itself; an environment contributes settings, never a rebuild.
  • R4 — Position is knowable. Any environment can state which version it runs, and the statement is trustworthy because promotion is what updates it.
  • R5 — Rollback is one move where the system operates. Returning an environment the system runs to a previous version is the same kind of action as promotion, not a reconstruction.
  • R6 — The operated path is exercised. Promotion in the environments the system runs happens routinely enough that its first use in anger is not its first use.
  • R7 — The hand-over is complete. What the system gives an environment it does not operate is enough to promote from without the system's help: the artifact, its provenance, and the settings channel — no oral tradition about extra steps only the builders know.
path: 024. A validated release is promoted by a declared path

items.title: Alternatives
items.text:
The chosen shape is the Decision: name the operated environments, delegate the rest. It satisfies every requirement — R2, R5, and R6 speak only of the environments the system runs, and R7 is the contract it keeps toward the ones it does not. The rejected shapes:

Alternative Why it fails Hand deployment (the status quo) R1: the set of environments is never written down. R7: the hand-over is oral tradition — the extra steps live in the heads of whoever built them. Per-environment build pipelines R3: the artifact in the environment was never the artifact that was validated, quietly undoing the confidence the release was built to carry. R5 as a side effect: rollback means waiting on a rebuild. Declare every environment out of scope R1 even for the environments the system does operate: development and test exist and are exercised daily, and leaving them unnamed makes the taught path a secret. The Decision takes this alternative's honest half — the further environments are not the spine's to operate — and refuses its dishonest half, which is silence about the two that are. A platform's native deployment model, wholesale R2 and R4 for one environment shape; fails R3's neutrality by binding promotion to that platform, which narrows where the system may run at all. Do nothing The current state described as a choice: every requirement left to oral tradition. This record exists to prevent that.
path: 024. A validated release is promoted by a declared path

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 024. A validated release is promoted by a declared path

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• The boundary between what the system operates and what it hands over is written down, so neither a reader nor a reviewer has to guess (R1, R4).
  • The two operated environments are exercised daily rather than hoped for (R6).
  • The hand-over contract is small and checkable: a signed, versioned artifact configured only by settings (R3).
path: 024. A validated release is promoted by a declared path

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• The system cannot promise a deployment how its release will be promoted; a customer who expects one must be told the answer is theirs to build.
  • Naming the operated environments constrains future flexibility — the point, but it will be felt as a cost.
  • The delegation is honest only while the handed-over artifact is truly complete: any property a deployment needs that the artifact lacks silently pulls the environment back into the spine (the system's kept core, 002)'s scope.
path: 024. A validated release is promoted by a declared path

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• Promotion of a released artifact beyond test has no mechanism here by design: a deployment that wants one writes it against the signed artifact, and the first such deployment is this record's first real test.
  • The image the pipeline validates and the image the release publishes are built by different steps, so R3 does not yet hold even for the named environments; closing that gap is a standing obligation of this record.
  • The cloud-provider runtime reaches neither named environment and runs today only in a local emulator, so its first real deployment will be unexercised.
  • Rollback beyond test is the deployment's move, named as a deploy-time act by the release record (019).
  • Settings are what an environment contributes to an artifact, and the channel that delivers them is already decided elsewhere (018).
  • Every environment must be reachable by the same identity rules that govern every other boundary (013).
path: 024. A validated release is promoted by a declared path

items.title: 025. Data has a stated lifetime that the system enforces
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Date: 2026-10-07
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

Acceptance trigger (swept 2026-10-19): increment 6.4 sets retention for catalogue data and operational signals and names the periods the record requires at acceptance; accepted in that pull request.

Every kind of data the system keeps has a stated lifetime, and the system enforces expiry on a schedule. A store with no stated lifetime is a defect: name the lifetime, or own "unbounded" in writing.
path: 025. Data has a stated lifetime that the system enforces

items.title: Decision
items.text:
Every kind of data has a named lifetime, and expiry is a mechanism. Data whose lifetime has passed is removed on schedule, without a person deciding per record. A store with no stated lifetime is treated as a defect: either its lifetime is named, or it is declared unbounded and the cost and risk of that are owned in writing.

No lifetime is stated or enforced anywhere today — operational data sits at library defaults, one signal's expiry is effectively switched off, and stored business data has no declared lifetime at all. This record is Proposed because the decision has not been made.
path: 025. Data has a stated lifetime that the system enforces

items.title: Context
items.text:
The system accumulates data in several kinds of place, each growing on its own schedule: operational signals from every part, business rows in stores. Growth is not neutral: storage has a cost that arrives as a bill or a full disk; old operational data keeps answering questions nobody asked anymore while burying the ones people do ask; and data that can identify people or customers creates obligations that grow with the time it is kept.

The system deliberately keeps all of this inside its own boundary — no operational data ships to a hosted service (016) — which means the organisation that runs the system owns the question of how long the data lives inside that boundary. That decision was named as the operator's problem when the boundary was drawn, and it has not been made since. The software's own defaults currently make that decision, and one of them is "keep it forever."

The default this record replaces: keep it forever

No expiry is a decision with a date on it — the day it bites is a full disk, a slow query, or an audit question about data the organisation should not hold. The record does not add risk by naming lifetimes; it removes the risk of the unnamed default.

The question this record answers is not which tool expires what. It is who says how long each kind of data is kept, what enforces the answer, and what happens when the answer changes.
path: 025. Data has a stated lifetime that the system enforces

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 Every kind has a stated lifetime. The period is written where a person answering "why do you still have this?" can read it. R2 Expiry is automatic. A mechanism on a schedule enforces the lifetime — nobody remembering to clean up. R3 Lifetimes differ by kind. Each kind has its own reason to keep or drop; one global number answers three questions badly. R4 The statement is answerable. "How long do we keep X?" is answered from the system's configuration, not a person's memory. R5 Change is a recorded change. Extending or shortening is deliberate and reviewable, not a side effect of upgrading a tool. R6 Cheap to keep true. A new store inherits a stated default lifetime rather than arriving undeclared.
path: 025. Data has a stated lifetime that the system enforces

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Upstream defaults (status quo) R1: the lifetime is whatever a vendor chose, which nobody read. R4: the answer requires auditing every tool's configuration. R2 fails in one place today, where the default is effectively no expiry. Keep everything forever The simplest policy to state and the most expensive to hold: R1's purpose — a lifetime of infinity is the absence of a decision. Cost grows without limit, and exposure of anything personal is maximised. Periodic manual cleanup R2 by definition, R4: what was pruned and when lives in their notes. R5 in practice: the cleanup skipped during a busy month is a silent policy change. One global retention number Easy to state and audit; R3: debug traces and customer records do not share a reason to exist, and one number is always wrong for at least one kind — too long for the sensitive, too short for the useful. Do nothing Costs nothing today and lets every vendor make the decision per upgrade. Every requirement fails by leaving the question unasked — the current state described as a choice.
path: 025. Data has a stated lifetime that the system enforces

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 025. Data has a stated lifetime that the system enforces

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• The organisation can answer retention questions about its own data without an audit (R1, R4).
  • Storage cost becomes bounded and predictable: growth is matched by enforced expiry (R2).
  • The exposure that comes with keeping data is limited to a chosen period (R3); retention changes become visible decisions (R5).
path: 025. Data has a stated lifetime that the system enforces

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• Enforced expiry destroys data irreversibly: a wrong lifetime is discovered after the fact — the failure is losing something that mattered, which argues for starting generous and tightening.
  • Every store's expiry is one more mechanism to operate and verify.
  • A stated lifetime invites exceptions: they must be refused or recorded, not absorbed.
path: 025. Data has a stated lifetime that the system enforces

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• The boundary inside which these lifetimes apply is drawn by 016, which names retention as the operator's problem and hands it to this record.
  • The lifetime of business rows interacts with schema change (023): deleting old rows is easy, deleting old shapes is a migration.
  • The periods themselves — the actual numbers — belong to whoever owns each kind of data and must be named when this record is accepted, not later.
  • Queued events: the reasoning for them stands, and the streaming slice that carried them left with the catalogue's scope (050); if a queue returns, an event lifetime shorter than the slowest consumer's recovery window turns retention into a delivery question owned by 027.
Why is 'unbounded' allowed at all?

Because pretending every store expires is how stores end up expiring by accident. Declaring a store unbounded forces the cheap conversation — cost, exposure, an owner in writing (R1) — that "nobody set a TTL" avoids. The defect is the undeclared default, not the length.
path: 025. Data has a stated lifetime that the system enforces

items.title: 026. The system can be brought back from a named snapshot
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Date: 2026-10-07
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

Acceptance trigger (swept 2026-10-19): increment 6.4 lands Elasticsearch snapshots and the first rehearsed restore (R2 is a demonstration, not a document); accepted in that pull request, writing the procedure into the resilience tree as it fills.

Durable data is backed up on a stated schedule, and recovery is a rehearsed path to a named point in time. Data deliberately not backed up is declared disposable in writing — "we would lose that" is a decision, not a discovery.
path: 026. The system can be brought back from a named snapshot

items.title: Decision
items.text:
Backups on a schedule; recovery by rehearsal. The durable data of the system is protected by backups taken on a stated schedule, and the system can be brought back to a named point in time by a declared procedure, not by improvisation. Data deliberately not backed up is declared disposable in writing, so "we would lose that" is a decision rather than a discovery.

Nothing is backed up today and no restore path exists. The only protection in the system is that storage volumes survive a container being recreated — an accident of tooling, not a decision. This record is Proposed because the decision, and the mechanism, do not yet exist.
path: 026. The system can be brought back from a named snapshot

items.title: Context
items.text:
The system stores things that took time to accumulate: business rows, the configuration that makes it run, the identity data that lets people in. None of it is reproducible from the codebase — the codebase reproduces the machinery, never the data. A lost database today is not an outage with a recovery; it is a permanent loss whose size nobody has measured, because nobody has been asked what would be lost.

The system is deliberately runnable in many places — one machine (006), the pipeline, a customer's environment — and each raises the same question: when the storage behind it is lost, what comes back, how much is missing, who performs the return. A host failure, a bad migration, a deleted volume: none require malice, and the system answers all three the same way — it does not come back.

Recovery is also a trust question. "What happens to our data if the worst happens?" is a question every operator and many customers ask, and an honest answer requires that someone has decided what is backed up, how often, and how it comes back — and has practised the coming-back part, because a restore nobody has rehearsed is only a hope.
path: 026. The system can be brought back from a named snapshot

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 Every durable store is covered or declared. Backed up on a stated schedule, or explicitly disposable — no third, unexamined category. R2 A restore produces a working system. Backups into a clean environment yield a running, consistent system — demonstrated, not assumed. R3 Loss is bounded and stated. The maximum data a failure can cost is a named number, chosen rather than discovered. R4 Recovery stays inside the boundary. Backups are operational data and live inside the system's boundary, not a third party's convenience (016). R5 The path is written where it can be found. The recovery procedure speaks the system's language, not one person's memory. R6 Cheap enough to actually run. Backups are automatic; the schedule and the success check are the system's job. R7 Recovery time is bounded and stated. How long a bring-back takes is a named number, measured by rehearsal, not estimated in the incident.
path: 026. The system can be brought back from a named snapshot

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Nothing (the status quo) Zero cost today; the loss is discovered at the worst moment. R1: the unexamined category is everything. R2: there is nothing to rehearse. The current arrangement, described as an option. Volume snapshots treated as backups Easy and automatic; R2 as usually practised: a snapshot of a running database is not a consistent database, and a snapshot set nobody has restored is untested until needed. R4's intent, when the snapshot lives wherever the platform puts it. Backups without rehearsed restore R2: the gap between "we have files" and "the system comes back" is exactly the gap rehearsals find. R5 usually follows: the unpractised restore procedure stays unwritten. Full disaster-recovery infrastructure A warm standby answers R2 and shrinks R3 — at the cost of operating the system twice. For a system whose recovery point is "everything," the cheap win is backups and a rehearsed restore; a standby is a different decision with a different price, not required here. Do nothing, honestly labelled Declaring the data disposable is legitimate while every database is a development database — recorded as the decision it is (R1's written declaration), and revisited the first time real data arrives.
path: 026. The system can be brought back from a named snapshot

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 026. The system can be brought back from a named snapshot

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• Loss stops being unbounded and starts being a chosen number (R3), and so does the time to recover (R7).
  • Recovery becomes a procedure with a known duration instead of an incident with an unknown one (R2, R5).
  • The trust question can be answered honestly to anyone who asks (R1, R4).
path: 026. The system can be brought back from a named snapshot

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• Backups are a standing cost that visibly pays for nothing on every day they are not needed — which is exactly why they decay. R6 and rehearsal are the defence, and they are the parts people skip.
  • A backup is a copy of the data, so the boundary rule (R4) applies to it too, including who may read it.
  • Rehearsing recovery is real time spent on a path the system hopes not to walk.
path: 026. The system can be brought back from a named snapshot

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• The recovery point and recovery time numbers belong to whoever accepts this record and must be named at acceptance, not deferred.
  • Backups of operational signals interact with their stated lifetimes (025): a backup older than a retention period is a contradiction waiting to be found.
  • A restore lands on a schema version, making this record a consumer of the migration path (023).
  • The placeholder pages on backup and disaster recovery under the architecture section remain headings until this record is accepted and they are written from its answer.
Why rehearse a restore we hope never to run?

Because R2 is the requirement rehearsal satisfies, and it cannot be satisfied by a document. Files that exist are not a system that comes back — the gap between them is where unpractised restores fail, and the only honest time to find that gap is a scheduled afternoon, not the incident.
path: 026. The system can be brought back from a named snapshot

items.title: 027. Every stream carries a stated delivery guarantee
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Date: 2026-10-07
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise
path: 027. Every stream carries a stated delivery guarantee

items.title: Decision
items.text:
Every stream of business events has a stated delivery guarantee — what the system promises about duplication and loss — and the parts that write and read the stream are configured to honour that promise rather than to whatever their libraries default to. Where a duplicate or a lost event would cost the business, the guarantee is enforced by configuration a reviewer can see; messages that cannot be delivered are parked somewhere named, not dropped in silence.

Today no stream states a guarantee: producers run on library defaults, the key that would give per-entity ordering is chosen in a way that defeats it, and the one dead-letter path that exists is unconsumed. This record is Proposed because the guarantees, and the enforcement, have not been decided.
path: 027. Every stream carries a stated delivery guarantee

items.title: Context
items.text:
Business facts move between parts as events: something happened here, and everything downstream must learn about it. Once a fact travels over a network to code the same team will write later, in another language, the possibilities are not just "delivered" and "not delivered" — an event can arrive twice, arrive out of order relative to its siblings, or arrive never. The business does not get to skip this question; it can only answer it by default or by decision.

The system carries events today with the default answer, which is roughly "probably once, in no particular order, and good luck." That is harmless in a demonstration and misleading as a taught example, because the example is what a future reader copies. It is also invisible: nothing in the codebase states what a consumer may assume, so every consumer silently assumes the friendliest interpretation and discovers the truth during an incident.

Ordering deserves its own sentence because the system currently contradicts itself: the design guidance tells producers to key events by entity so each entity's history stays in order, while the shipped example keys every event randomly, which spreads one entity's events across every partition. A consumer that trusted the guidance would be wrong, and the guidance would not say so.

The question this record answers is what the system promises about events in flight — per stream, in writing, enforced where it matters.
path: 027. Every stream carries a stated delivery guarantee

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

  • R1 — The promise is stated per stream. For each stream, a reader can find what is guaranteed about duplication and loss, without asking a producer's author.
  • R2 — Configuration matches the promise. The settings on writers and readers are the ones that make the promise true; a default that contradicts the promise is a defect, not a shortcut.
  • R3 — Duplication is survivable where it is allowed. If a stream may duplicate, consumers can tell a repeat from a new fact; a duplicated event must not double-count in anything the business reads.
  • R4 — Order is promised where it matters. Where an entity's events have a meaningful sequence, the arrangement keeps one entity's events in that sequence end to end; where it does not, the stream says so.
  • R5 — Undeliverable events land somewhere named. A failure to deliver becomes a visible, inspectable pile with an owner, not a silent gap between what was sent and what arrived.
  • R6 — Cheap for the routine case. A new stream inherits the stated defaults rather than a library's, and stating its guarantee is one line a reviewer sees.
path: 027. Every stream carries a stated delivery guarantee

items.title: Alternatives
items.text:
• Library defaults (the status quo). Every part inherits whatever its client library chose. It fails R1 — the promise is unwritten and differs per language — and R2, because nobody checked the defaults against any intent. As a taught example it is the worst option: it teaches the question away.
  • Exactly-once everywhere. Strongest promise, and the libraries can deliver pieces of it. It fails R6: the machinery reaches into every writer, reader, and store, and it buys a guarantee the demonstration streams do not need — a promise the business cannot yet name a cost for. Strongest is not the same as correct.
  • At-least-once with idempotent consumers. Deliver duplicates, make duplicates harmless. It satisfies R1, R2, R3, and R6 with modest machinery, and it is the honest shape of what the system's storage sinks already do by accident — upserting by identifier makes a redelivered event a no-op. It fails R4 unless keying is fixed, which is exactly the contradiction this record names.
  • Best-effort, declared. Some streams genuinely do not care — a lost telemetry event is not a business loss. Declaring that is legitimate and passes R1; it fails R3 and R5 only if applied to streams that do care, which is the decision this record forces per stream.
  • Do nothing. Costs nothing and leaves every consumer to assume the friendliest reading of an unwritten promise; it fails R1 by definition and teaches the gap to everyone who copies the example.
path: 027. Every stream carries a stated delivery guarantee

items.title: Tradeoffs
items.text:
• Positive: consumers can reason about what they will receive instead of hoping (R1, R2); duplicate-tolerance becomes a designed property of the sinks that need it rather than an accident of upserts (R3); the ordering guidance and the shipped example stop contradicting each other (R4); delivery failures become visible work rather than missing rows (R5).
  • Negative: every guarantee has a price in throughput, latency, or machinery, and naming a guarantee per stream forces that price to be paid and argued rather than dodged; idempotent consumers must carry a notion of "already seen," which is state they did not need before; and a parked pile of undeliverable events (R5) is a queue with a human attached — someone owns reading it, or it becomes a landfill.
  • Neutral / follow-ups: the shipped example currently keys events randomly while the design guidance prescribes keying by entity — closing that contradiction is this record's first act on acceptance, in whichever direction the guarantee for that stream turns out to be; the dead-letter path that exists today has no consumer and no replay procedure, and R5 is not satisfied until parked events can be inspected and returned; stream retention is a delivery question, not only a storage one — a lifetime shorter than the slowest consumer's recovery window silently breaks the guarantee, and lifetimes are owned by 025; the compatibility of what the events contain is decided elsewhere (017) and this record covers only how the containing stream behaves; the name a stream — or a dead-letter stream — carries is set by the naming convention (032); and authentication of the parts that speak to the stream belongs to 013.
path: 027. Every stream carries a stated delivery guarantee

items.title: 028. Operational secret handling has a named owner and a rehearsed path
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-07
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

Accepted 2026-10-19: the owner of secret handling is the maintainers team (the role that signs changes under 044). The urgent-rotation, key-loss, and break-glass paths are written in Operations Ownership, with the first rehearsal scheduled there (R3). Membership on the accepted side already works: adding a person is a reviewed change to .sops.yaml plus automated re-encryption (008).

The bad cases of secret handling — urgent rotation, key loss, break-glass, removal — have a named owner and written, rehearsed paths. No secret is in a state where nobody knows who could rotate or recover it.
path: 028. Operational secret handling has a named owner and a rehearsed path

items.title: Decision
items.text:
Handling is owned, written, rehearsed. Rotating a secret, replacing a key, recovering a lost one, granting temporary access, removing a person: each is owned by a named role and follows a written path walked before it is needed.

The storage mechanism (008) decides how secrets are stored; this record decides who operates it, on what rhythm, and what happens in the bad cases. No secret, and no key, may be in a state where nobody knows who could rotate or recover it.
path: 028. Operational secret handling has a named owner and a rehearsed path

items.title: Context
items.text:
Secrets are encrypted to a named set of people and travel with the code as ciphertext. Membership is already a working process — adding a person is a reviewed change, the re-encryption that follows is automated. That is the easy direction: planned, reviewed, rehearsed by frequency.

The hard cases had no owner:

  • A credential must be rotated today — suspected leak, departing person, vendor's forced expiry. Who acts, how fast, and how does the new value travel without a group chat?
  • A person loses their key. Is the data recoverable, by whom, under whose judgement — or is the honest answer that it is not?
  • An incident needs an outsider to read one secret right now. Is there a path, and does anyone find out afterwards?
  • Do the keys themselves, and the automation's shared secret, ever get replaced — or only added to?

None of these are storage problems — the ciphertext is fine. They are organisational problems, and the record that drew the storage line named them as undecided. The risk of leaving them undecided is specific: when the bad case arrives, the path gets invented under pressure, and an invented path around a security mechanism is how that mechanism gets bypassed for good.
path: 028. Operational secret handling has a named owner and a rehearsed path

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 An owner exists. One named role answers for rotation, keys, membership, and the bad cases — a written answer to "who would do this?" R2 Urgent rotation is a rehearsed path. Replaced and redistributed quickly, by the owner, walked at least once before it was needed. R3 Loss has a declared answer. Recovery with named custodians, or declared unrecoverable with the consequence owned. Silence is not a third option. R4 Temporary access is possible and visible. A break-glass grant for a stated reason and period, leaving a trace the owner reviews. R5 Removal is effective, not cosmetic. Future access stops; the record says what removal does not fix — what that person already copied. R6 Keys and automation secrets are themselves rotated. A stated replacement cadence, or a stated reason not. R7 Cheap enough to survive. Routine handling stays one reviewed change with automated follow-through; a path heavier than the mechanism it governs will be bypassed — that counts as this record failing.
path: 028. Operational secret handling has a named owner and a rehearsed path

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Leave it undecided (status quo) R1 by construction; everything else by postponement: the path will be invented during the incident that needed an owner. The current arrangement, and the reason this record exists. A dedicated secrets platform Answers R2, R4, R6 well as product features. Fails R7 for a system of this size today — a second platform to operate, with its own custody question about its root — and does not answer R3 or R5 by itself: custody and offboarding remain organisational decisions wearing new software. A legitimate destination, not an automatic one. Ad-hoc handling by senior people What happens today: whoever built the mechanism gets paged. R1: the role is a person, and people leave. R2: an unpractised path is slower and less safe. R4: informal access leaves no trace. Strictest-possible policy No break-glass, no escrow, no exceptions. R4: an incident that cannot grant access does not stop needing the secret — it stops using the mechanism. R3: declaring data unrecoverable is only honest if the business agreed to lose it. Do nothing, recorded honestly "Lost keys mean lost data; urgent rotation means whoever is available" is legitimate at this size — written with R1–R3 answered in the negative and the risk named, not left as silence.
path: 028. Operational secret handling has a named owner and a rehearsed path

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 028. Operational secret handling has a named owner and a rehearsed path

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• The bad cases stop being improvisations: rotation, loss, and break-glass have owners and paths before they are needed (R1–R4).
  • Offboarding means something honest, including about what removal cannot undo (R5).
  • The storage rule finally has its operational half: the two records together describe a usable mechanism, not a vault nobody can open in an emergency.
path: 028. Operational secret handling has a named owner and a rehearsed path

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• A named owner is a single point unless the path is documented well enough to hand over: the record trades silence for a dependency on a role.
  • Rehearsing urgent rotation is time spent pretending to have an incident.
  • Every added control — trails, cadences, grants — is friction that, per R7, must stay lighter than the risk it manages, or people route around it.
path: 028. Operational secret handling has a named owner and a rehearsed path

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• The storage rule names this exact gap as its open end (008) — acceptance closes it here.
  • Service identity assumes credentials are "issued, stored, and rotated by the arrangements the system runs" (013) — this record is where those arrangements get their owner.
  • The cadence numbers, custodian counts, and grant durations are named in the Operations Ownership guide, not deferred.
  • The automation's own shared secret sits in R6 explicitly so it cannot stay in the unexamined category.
Why rehearse paths for incidents that may never happen?

Because the first real run is the worst day to learn the procedure: a suspected leak is a Tuesday afternoon, not a project. A path walked once in calm conditions is minutes; an invented path under pressure is the mechanism getting bypassed for good (R2, R3).
path: 028. Operational secret handling has a named owner and a rehearsed path

items.title: 029. What ships is signed, and its origin can be proven
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-07
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

Every released part is signed at publication, carries its build provenance and contents inventory, and the release event ends by verifying the signature against a pinned identity. Anyone can prove who built an artifact, without trusting a copy.
path: 029. What ships is signed, and its origin can be proven

items.title: Decision
items.text:
Sign, attest, verify — at publication. Every deployable part of a release is signed, its build origin recorded alongside it, and its inventory of contents attached — and the release is not delivered until the signature has been verified against the identity that was supposed to produce it. Anyone holding a released artifact can prove which pipeline run produced it and what it contains, without trusting a copy of the artifact or the word of whoever delivered it.

This decision was in force before it was written down: publication signs each artifact without holding a secret of its own, attaches provenance and contents as attestations, and ends with a verification step pinned to the exact identity allowed to have produced the release. This record exists because a mechanism this load-bearing should not be folklore.
path: 029. What ships is signed, and its origin can be proven

items.title: Context
items.text:
A released artifact travels: pushed to a registry, pulled by environments, copied by pipelines, sometimes mirrored to places the organisation does not operate. At every hop the receiving side asks — is this the thing we published, a copy, or something wearing its name? — and an artifact with no answer is trusted only as far as the last person who touched it.

The system releases as one versioned whole (019), and the unit that ships is the unit that was validated (010). Both properties depend on the artifact a consumer runs being the artifact the pipeline produced. Without signatures and provenance, that identity is an assumption renewed at every pull; with them, it is a check.

An assumption renewed at every pull

Each hop — registry, mirror, cache, laptop — is a place an artifact can be swapped or mislabelled, and the puller has no memory of the pipeline. Without a signature the consumer re-trusts from scratch every time, silently; a verified signature and provenance statement turn that trust into a check the puller runs and records.

The supply chain the artifacts are built from is scanned and reported elsewhere (015 — the scanning half); this record covers the other half: the trustworthiness of what the organisation itself publishes. There is also a teaching obligation: the examples are how the organisation teaches (009), and publication without proof would teach that shipping ends at uploading bytes.
path: 029. What ships is signed, and its origin can be proven

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 Every released part is covered. Signing and origin proof apply to every deployable part automatically — triggered by being a part. R2 No secret to steal. The proof of who published does not depend on a custodyed signing key that, leaked, lets anyone publish a trusted forgery. R3 Contents travel with the artifact. What a part is built from is attached: "what is in what we ran?" is a lookup, not a reconstruction. R4 Verification is part of delivery. The release event checks the signature against a pinned identity; delivery without verification is incomplete. R5 The check needs no insider. A consumer with no special access can verify the signature and read the provenance and inventory. R6 Cheap to keep true. A new deployable part gets the whole chain by convention, no per-part ceremony.
path: 029. What ships is signed, and its origin can be proven

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Publish unsigned Simplest, and the norm for internal systems. R1's purpose: consumers cannot tell the published artifact from a forgery. R3: contents knowledge exists only in build logs that expire. R4 becomes impossible — there is nothing to verify. A long-lived signing key Classical and portable; R2 fails — the key becomes a crown jewel with a custody problem attached (the class of problem 028 handles), and a leaked key forges trust retroactively, since old verification still accepts it. Keyless publication removes the asset instead of guarding it. Sign only, no provenance A signature answers "who" but not "how" or "what." R3, and R5 weakened: the consumer can confirm the publisher yet cannot say what the artifact contains without re-running the build. Verify at the deployment site only R4's spirit, not its letter: the release event would complete unverified. R5 in practice: verification rules known only to deployers are not usable by other consumers. Do nothing (keep the mechanism undocumented) Fails no requirement of the mechanism, and fails the organisation's: an unrecorded load-bearing decision is silently dropped by the next person who rewrites the pipeline, and its absence would not fail any check.
path: 029. What ships is signed, and its origin can be proven

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 029. What ships is signed, and its origin can be proven

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• Artifact identity survives every copy and mirror (R1, R5).
  • There is no signing key to guard, leak, or rotate (R2).
  • Incident response can ask what a running part contains and get an attached answer (R3).
  • The release is self-certifying — delivery includes its own proof (R4).
path: 029. What ships is signed, and its origin can be proven

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• The proof depends on external parties — the identity issuer and the public record — so a release cannot be signed where they are unreachable: a network dependency on the one step that must never be improvised.
  • Keyless signatures age differently from keys: long-term verification of old releases relies on those parties' history staying intact.
  • Signature and provenance say who and how, not whether it is safe — a signed artifact is a truthful one, not a clean one, and the scanning question stays separate (015).
path: 029. What ships is signed, and its origin can be proven

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• Signing runs only at release: an artifact built outside a release event is unsigned by design and must not be confused with a release.
  • The verification identity is pinned to the release workflow itself — a change to that workflow's path or name is a change to the trust anchor and deserves the review weight of a security boundary.
  • Promotion of a verified artifact into environments is where this record stops and 024 begins.
  • The contents inventory is assembled from two sources — the runtime image and the built application, merged into one document — for the one part whose build produces an application inventory; every other part's inventory comes from its image alone, and a new kind of deployable part must name how its inventory is produced.
  • R5's no-insider check assumes the registry serves signatures, provenance, and inventories to anyone — a registry setting not yet declared anywhere beside it.
Why keyless signing instead of an organisation key?

Because an organisation key is an asset that, leaked, forges trust retroactively — and guarding it is a custody problem (028) that never ends. Keyless signing ties each signature to the pipeline identity that made it, so there is no key to steal and the forgery scenario has no object (R2).
path: 029. What ships is signed, and its origin can be proven

items.title: 030. Interfaces between parts are verified, not assumed
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-07
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

Accepted 2026-10-19: for the catalogue's public interface, the checking mechanism is the parity harness — the agreement is stated once, in scenarios read from the reference source and cited (052), and drift fails the change (R1, R4). Internal interfaces are typed imports inside one repository (001), so consumers are not hand-mirrored (R2). Named gap: the template example frontend's hand-written TS mirror is unverified — a deviation that ends with the example's removal (DD-019); the Atlas dashboard is vendored and out of scope (R3).

Where a part offers an interface another consumes, the agreement is stated once and checked: a change that breaks a consumer fails where it is made, not where it is felt. The check remembers what the provider sends, so consumers do not have to.
path: 030. Interfaces between parts are verified, not assumed

items.title: Decision
items.text:
The agreement is stated once, and a check enforces it. Where one part offers an interface another consumes, the agreement between them lives in one place and is checked, so a change that breaks a consumer is caught where it is made, not where it is felt. A consumer does not rely on remembering what the provider sends — the check remembers for it.

The domain concepts behind these interfaces already have one canonical definition (004); this record covers the interfaces themselves — the callable surface a consumer actually depends on.
path: 030. Interfaces between parts are verified, not assumed

items.title: Context
items.text:
The system's parts talk over interfaces: screens call services, services call services, and the shapes crossing those boundaries are the business concepts. An interface is a promise in both directions — the provider promises what it returns, the consumer promises what it sends — and a promise only one side wrote down is a promise nobody enforces.

Right now each side writes its own version. The provider declares what it serves; the consumer re-declares by hand what it believes the provider serves. Nothing compares the two. The provider publishes a machine-readable description and a test confirms it exists — but nothing downstream reads it, so the description can say one thing while the consumer assumes another, and both are green.

That is the shared-domain-model failure (004) one layer out: a concept can be canonical and still be transported wrongly, because the transport agreement is folklore on both sides.

The cost lands predictably: a provider renames a field, changes a type, makes it absent — every consumer that assumed the old shape keeps compiling and starts failing at runtime, in a screen a person is looking at, far from the change. More consumers, more copies, more coordination exercises per change.

One fact makes fixing this cheap here: every consumer lives in the same repository as the provider it reads (001), so finding them is a search, not a campaign. The arrangement that makes interface verification expensive in a distributed estate is absent — which is why these requirements are worth meeting at the cheapest point, before the estate grows.
path: 030. Interfaces between parts are verified, not assumed

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 The agreement is stated once. One place says what the interface is; provider and consumer both answer to it. R2 Drift fails the change that caused it. A check at commit or review time, not a runtime discovery. R3 Consumers are found, not remembered. Dependents identifiable mechanically; "did we get everyone?" has an answer. R4 The agreement is readable by whoever integrates. What it accepts and returns, without reading provider source. R5 Compatible change stays cheap. An optional element costs a small step, not a regeneration ceremony. R6 The check is honest about what it covers. An unchecked interface is named as unchecked — no false confidence.
path: 030. Interfaces between parts are verified, not assumed

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Hand-mirrored interfaces (status quo) R1 by construction, R2 completely: nothing compares the two statements, so drift is invisible until runtime. R3: finding consumers means searching for copies of a shape and hoping the search was clever enough. Generate consumers from the provider's description R1, R3, R4, R5 elegantly. R2 on its own: generation proves the consumer matches the description, not that the provider honours it. R6 fails unless the description is a contract with teeth, not documentation with a syntax. Assumes every consumer tolerates a generated shape — a user-facing interface often won't. Contract tests between the sides R2 and R6 directly; survives a provider that won't publish a description. R1 as usually practised: expectations live in consumer tests, so the agreement is written N times. R4: a test suite is not a document an integrator can read. Coordination by review R2 and R3 exactly as often as reviewers are new, tired, or far from the other stack — which, in a system spanning several languages on one machine (006), is often. The current arrangement with a title. Do nothing Keeps every interface change a runtime discovery. R1–R4 by leaving the agreement unwritten and unchecked — the state described as an option.
path: 030. Interfaces between parts are verified, not assumed

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 030. Interfaces between parts are verified, not assumed

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• Interface breakage moves from user screens to the change that caused it (R2).
  • Consumers of a change are enumerable rather than remembered (R3).
  • Integrators get a readable statement instead of an archaeology project (R4).
  • The shared-concept decision finally covers how concepts travel, not only what they are.
path: 030. Interfaces between parts are verified, not assumed

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• The agreement becomes a maintained artifact — and a stale agreement is worse than none, because it is trusted.
  • Generation trades hand-written consumer code for generated code that must be lived with; user-facing shapes resist being generated.
  • Enforcement needs a checking point; the accepted mechanism (the parity harness, R1/R4) covers the public interface, and the remaining gap is named below rather than papered over.
path: 030. Interfaces between parts are verified, not assumed

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• The provider's machine-readable description and the test that only confirms it exists are the seed for a comparison check where the parity harness does not apply (R6).
  • Which representations are generated versus hand-kept (004) is answered here for interfaces only; how an interface changes without breaking readers is governed by 017 — this record adds verification, not direction. How the concepts travel over streams — ordering and duplication — is owned by 027; the streaming slice left with the catalogue's scope (050).
Why is a published OpenAPI description not enough?

A description that nothing compares against is a claim, not a check. The provider can publish a description that disagrees with its own code, and a consumer's hand-written mirror can disagree with both — all green (R2). The check must compare provider-against-statement and consumer-against-statement; publishing one side's belief is step one, not the mechanism.
path: 030. Interfaces between parts are verified, not assumed

items.title: 031. Language and runtime versions have a declared support window
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-07
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

Accepted 2026-10-19: the window is declared in Runtime Windows — one answer per runtime, the pin files named, major bumps by reviewed change of the maintainers team. R2 was closed in the same sweep: the dev container pinned Node to the moving lts tag while the dashboard build pinned 24; both now pin 24.

For every runtime the system runs on, the organisation declares a support window, and every place a version is written agrees with it. A major-version move is a planned, recorded act — never something that happens by accident because one machine upgraded first.
path: 031. Language and runtime versions have a declared support window

items.title: Decision
items.text:
A window per runtime, written down. For every language and runtime, the organisation declares the versions it undertakes to build, test, and keep working — a floor, a ceiling, an owner for bumps. Every place a version is written agrees with that declaration, and a disagreement is caught, not discovered.

A major move is planned work. Moving a runtime's major version is a scheduled, recorded act with an owner and an end date for the old version — never a surprise delivered by an upgrade or an image refresh.
path: 031. Language and runtime versions have a declared support window

items.title: Context
items.text:
The system spans several languages, and each version is a business fact, not a technicality: it determines which libraries can be used, which security fixes arrive, what a joiner installs, and how long before the organisation runs something the ecosystem stopped maintaining. A runtime past end of support is a compliance conversation and an emergency upgrade, in that order.

Because the whole system releases as one versioned whole (019), a runtime version is a property of the system, not of a part — which means it needs one answer.

It had several: the same runtime's version appears in the build definition, the development environment, the shipped image, and the compiler configuration, kept by nobody in step — the development environment asked for the Node "lts" release while the build and image pinned a major, tools were pinned to "latest", and two compiler targets disagreed. Nothing caught the disagreement, because nothing stated what the answer was supposed to be.

Two neighbouring records bound this one: keeping dependencies up to date (020) covers the libraries inside a runtime; this record speaks to the runtime itself, which that record does not — a language major version is not a dependency bump, because it can change what correct code is. Where they meet — a runtime minor release is arguably a dependency update — the owner of that bump is named in the window.

The development environment is a versioned artifact (011) — that record decides the environment is reproducible; this one decides what version it is allowed to contain, and who says so.
path: 031. Language and runtime versions have a declared support window

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 The window is written. The supported range per runtime, readable without inspecting five configuration files. R2 One answer everywhere. Every place a version is declared agrees with the window; a disagreement is caught by a check, not an incident. R3 Nothing floats. No runtime, tool, or compiler target unpinned — an unpinned thing changes without a decision. R4 Bumps are planned. Scheduled work with an owner and an end date for the old version. R5 Support status is visible. How close each runtime is to losing upstream maintenance, without research. R6 Cheap for the routine case. A patch or minor inside the window is automatic; only a window change costs a decision.
path: 031. Language and runtime versions have a declared support window

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Pins without a window (status quo) R1: the window exists only as an archaeology result. R2: the disagreement observed today. R3 wherever a tool is pinned to "latest". Track the newest of everything R4: "always newest" is a policy of never planning, and every major becomes an emergency when it lands. It quietly narrows where the system can run — consumers and hosts on older supported versions excluded by choice nobody made. Freeze with long windows R5's purpose: a long window with no plan for its end is how an organisation ends up two majors behind with a deadline. It collides with dependency currency (020), which commits to staying near the front. Let each part choose its version R1 and R2 at the level that matters: as many answers as parts, and a release that can no longer be described in one version number. Do nothing Free today; the observed drift continues, and the first end-of-support date arrives as news. It fails every requirement by leaving the window unwritten — which describes today's drift as if it were a choice.
path: 031. Language and runtime versions have a declared support window

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 031. Language and runtime versions have a declared support window

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• "What version do we support?" has one written answer (R1), and every configuration file is accountable to it (R2).
  • Runtime upgrades become scheduled work with a visible deadline (R4).
  • End-of-support risk stops being discovered by an auditor (R5).
path: 031. Language and runtime versions have a declared support window

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• A declared window is a commitment that costs effort at its edges: supporting the floor of a window is real work a single pinned version would dodge.
  • Reconciling the places versions are written touches build, environment, image, and compiler configuration together — exactly the cross-stack coordination this system keeps minimal.
  • A window written but not reviewed is worse than none, because people trust it.
path: 031. Language and runtime versions have a declared support window

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• The remaining pin drifts are the first items the window check must catch: the base TypeScript target (es2015 in tsconfig.base.json) against the per-project targets (es2022), and the dev container's SOPS feature pinned to latest (R3).
  • The window is revisited in the cadence review (015) — no separate review is invented for it.
  • The window's numbers — floor, ceiling, and how long an old major stays alive — are named in Runtime Windows, not deferred.
Why a window instead of one pinned version?

One pin answers "what do we run," not "what do we support" (R1). Consumers, hosts, and onboarding need the range; a lone pin gives them a single point and hides the edges. The window also turns the floor into a commitment with a plan (R4) — a lone pin quietly ages into an end-of-support surprise.
path: 031. Language and runtime versions have a declared support window

items.title: 032. Shared streams are named by a declared convention
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-07
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise
path: 032. Shared streams are named by a declared convention

items.title: Decision
items.text:
The name of a stream that carries business events is chosen by a stated convention rather than by whoever creates it: the name says what the stream carries and which version of it, and it deliberately says nothing about which environment the stream lives in. A reader who can see a name can tell what flows through it and whether it is the current version, without asking.

The convention exists and is followed by the business streams it was written for; it has simply never been recorded as a decision, only written in guidance. This record promotes the convention to a decision so that it survives the guidance being rewritten, and so a name that ignores it is visibly a deviation rather than a second opinion. The few names that already ignore it are named as follow-ups rather than hidden.
path: 032. Shared streams are named by a declared convention

items.title: Context
items.text:
Streams are the seams between the system's parts, and unlike code, a stream name is not local to the change that creates it. A name is referenced by producers, consumers, connectors, configuration, dashboards, and operational runbooks, in several languages and the habits of whoever writes the next consumer, and it is very expensive to change once anything is attached to it. A stream created today with a name that describes its author's branch, or its environment, becomes a permanent artifact nobody can rename.

The organisation already chose a convention, and the business streams follow it: lowercase, component-separated names that read as what category, what thing, which version, with a length limit, and with an explicit decision not to encode the environment. That last choice is the load-bearing one: encoding an environment in a name means the same logical stream has different names in different places, which makes every producer and consumer configuration environment-specific and turns a portable system into a pile of per-place wiring. Keeping the environment out of the name is what lets the same definition travel.

None of this is written down as a decision. It lives in a guidance page, which means a future rewrite of that page can quietly reverse it, and a new stream can be named by instinct — including the environment-encoding the convention rejects — with nothing to point at. The question this record answers is what a stream name is allowed to say, and why.
path: 032. Shared streams are named by a declared convention

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

  • R1 — The name is self-describing. From the name alone, a reader can tell what the stream carries.
  • R2 — Version is part of identity. An incompatible change to what a stream carries produces a new name, so old and new can coexist without guessing.
  • R3 — Environment is not part of identity. The same logical stream has the same name everywhere it runs, so definitions travel between environments unchanged.
  • R4 — The convention is uniform. Every stream follows one shape, so a reader never has to learn a second naming style to read a list of streams.
  • R5 — The convention is stated where names are made. Whoever creates a stream meets the rule at that moment, not in a review comment later.
  • R6 — Cheap to keep true. Naming a new stream correctly is the default, not an extra step.
path: 032. Shared streams are named by a declared convention

items.title: Alternatives
items.text:
• Free naming. Fastest for whoever creates a stream, and the state without a convention. It fails R1, R2, and R4 immediately: a list of streams stops being readable, and incompatible shapes either collide under one name or hide under names that do not say they replaced anything.
  • Environment encoded in the name. Familiar, and tempting because it makes a running environment legible at a glance. It fails R3 directly: the same stream gains a different name per environment, so every producer, consumer, and connector needs environment-specific configuration — which contradicts the arrangement that settings, not names, are what differ between environments (018).
  • Central registry of stream names. A person or tool approves each name. It passes R4 by force and fails R6: naming a stream becomes a request, and requests during delivery get bypassed, which leaves the registry incomplete and the convention optional.
  • Convention by example only (the status quo). Guidance describes the shape and existing streams demonstrate it. It passes R1 and R2 in practice and fails R5 — guidance is read after the name is chosen, if at all — and leaves the whole convention one documentation rewrite away from being silently abandoned, which is the reason for this record.
  • Do nothing. Costs nothing and keeps the convention unwritten; it fails R5 by construction and R3 the first time someone encodes an environment because nothing said not to.
path: 032. Shared streams are named by a declared convention

items.title: Tradeoffs
items.text:
• Positive: a stream list is readable without a guide (R1, R4); an incompatible change gets a name that says so, which is what lets old and new readers coexist (R2); stream definitions are portable because the environment is not baked into them (R3); and the convention now has a record to be cited by, rather than a page that can be rewritten around.
  • Negative: names are longer and more formal than anyone's instinct, and the length limit occasionally forces an abbreviation that costs the self-describing property it exists to protect; a version suffix invites streams to be versioned reflexively rather than when a change genuinely breaks readers; and the convention is enforced by review rather than by a check, so a non-conforming name can still land — a named gap of this record rather than a tolerated state.
  • Neutral / follow-ups: what makes a change incompatible enough to deserve a new version is decided by the compatibility rule (017), and this record only supplies the name that change travels under; the guarantees carried inside a stream — duplication, ordering, undeliverable events — belong to 027, and the convention for dead-letter names follows the same shape as the stream it parks for; and a check that refuses a non-conforming name at creation is the enforcement point this record does not yet have, and should acquire. Six names in the repository already ignore the convention: three throwaway topics that end-to-end tests create, which read as one kebab-case phrase rather than the component shape, and three internal topics a connector names for itself, which also exceed the length limit. Whether the convention covers such throwaway and infrastructure topics — or whether they are explicitly out of scope — is not yet written down, and should be.
path: 032. Shared streams are named by a declared convention

items.title: 033. Shipped artifacts carry a contents inventory
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-07
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

Every deployable part carries a machine-readable inventory of its contents, attached at publication. "What is in what we ran?" is a lookup against the artifact, not a reconstruction from build logs.
path: 033. Shipped artifacts carry a contents inventory

items.title: Decision
items.text:
The inventory ships with the part. Every deployable part of a release carries a machine-readable inventory of what it contains, attached at publication in the same attestation step that carries its provenance (029). Answering "what is in what we ran?" — at an incident, during a recall of a flawed dependency, for a customer question — is a lookup, not a reconstruction.

This decision was in force before it was written down: publication assembles each part's inventory and attaches it to the signed artifact, and the advisory scans over released parts (015) consume it. This record exists because the inventory is what makes those scans answerable for a specific release, and that role should not be implicit.
path: 033. Shipped artifacts carry a contents inventory

items.title: Context
items.text:
A release is a set of artifacts that travel (019), and the unit that ships is the unit that was validated (010).

When a running part goes wrong, the first question is not who built it — that is provenance (029) — but what is inside it: which dependencies, which versions, which layers. A part whose contents can only be re-derived by re-running an old build — if the build inputs still exist at all — turns an urgent question into slow reconstruction work.

The organisation already answers dependency questions continuously for the codebase (015); the inventory makes the same answer specific to a released artifact rather than to the current branch. Origin and contents stay separate decisions, each checkable on its own: an artifact can have perfect provenance and no inventory, and the gap should be visible as exactly that.

Provenance and inventory: two answers, one attestation

Provenance (029) answers where this came from; the inventory answers what is inside it. They ship attached together, at the same signing step, and are checked apart — a CVE sweep reads the inventory, a trust decision reads the signature. Conflating them is how a scanned branch gets mistaken for an answered release.
path: 033. Shipped artifacts carry a contents inventory

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 Every released part is covered. An inventory is produced and attached for every deployable part, automatically. R2 The inventory travels with the artifact. Attached at publication, so it survives every copy and mirror the artifact survives. R3 Machines can read it. A standard machine-readable form: scanners, report builders, a customer's tooling — no cooperation needed. R4 Incident-time lookup. Contents readable the moment the question is asked, however old the release, without re-running its build. R5 Cheap to keep true. A new deployable part gets the inventory by convention, no ceremony.
path: 033. Shipped artifacts carry a contents inventory

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Contents live only in build logs R2 and R4: logs expire, are not attached, are written for humans. R3: no standard form. The arrangement this record replaces. Reconstruct contents on demand R4 under pressure: the worst moment to discover the old build inputs are gone — and it answers about today's toolchain, not what the release contained. Ship the inventory as a side document R2 in substance: a document beside the artifact is copied at some hops and not others, and nothing binds it to the artifact it describes. Rely on the registry's metadata The registry knows storage-level facts, not application contents, readable only through that registry. R3; the answer strands where the artifact was mirrored from. Do nothing (keep the inventory implicit) The state this record corrects. Fails the organisation's requirement: the next person to wire a new part would not know the inventory is required, and its absence would not fail any check.
path: 033. Shipped artifacts carry a contents inventory

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 033. Shipped artifacts carry a contents inventory

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• An incident question about a running part is answered by reading the artifact (R2, R4).
  • Dependency advisories are answered per release, not per branch — what 015 needs to be precise.
  • Consumers can run their own tooling over what they received (R3).
path: 033. Shipped artifacts carry a contents inventory

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• Assembling an inventory adds real time to every publication, and for the one part whose build already produces its own application inventory the two sources must be merged into one document — a maintained mechanism.
  • An inventory is a claim about contents, not about safety: the judgement of whether any of it is a problem stays with the scanning record (015).
path: 033. Shipped artifacts carry a contents inventory

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• The two-source merge (runtime image plus built application) exists for the one part whose build produces an application inventory; every other part's inventory comes from its image alone, and a new kind of deployable part must name how its inventory is produced rather than assume the image covers it.
  • Reading an inventory with no special access depends on the registry serving attached attestations to anyone — the same undeclared registry setting 029 waits on; confirm it before R2's no-insider reading is called met.
  • A publication-time inventory is silent about contents added later at run time — configuration, downloads, mounted code — outside what any inventory can claim.
path: 033. Shipped artifacts carry a contents inventory

items.title: 034. Signals meet at one replaceable collection point
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-07
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

Every part exports its three signals to one collection point over a standard protocol. The tools that store and display the picture live behind that seam and can be changed without touching a part.
path: 034. Signals meet at one replaceable collection point

items.title: Decision
items.text:
One seam, one protocol. Every part exports the same three signals — traces, metrics, and logs — to one collection point that is part of the system, over a standard protocol, and never to a storage or visualisation backend directly. The collection point is the single seam: the tools that store and display the picture live behind it and can be changed without touching the parts.

This decision was in force before it was written down: the observability stack the development arrangement starts (006) includes a collection point that every instrumented part exports to, and the backends behind it are known to the parts only through it.

Where the picture is allowed to live — inside the system, never with a vendor — is a separate decision (016); this record covers the shape of the seam the signals pass through.
path: 034. Signals meet at one replaceable collection point

items.title: Context
items.text:
The running picture is assembled from what every part emits, and the organisation has to decide how the emissions reach the tools. The two failure shapes are known: parts that point directly at their storage backends, so changing a backend means touching every part, and parts that each speak a different tool's protocol, so the picture cannot be assembled at all. Both are the absence of a seam.

016 decides the picture is produced and consumed inside the system. That is compatible with several internal shapes — every part wired to its own storage, one shared collector, a sidecar per part — and the shape is a real decision with its own consequences: it determines what it costs to change an observation tool, and what it costs to instrument a new part.

Separating the two records keeps each checkable on its own: a system can keep its data inside the boundary and still have no seam, and the gap should be visible as exactly that.

A standard protocol at the seam is what makes the arrangement portable. It is also the condition under which a future production arrangement could export elsewhere without re-instrumenting the parts — a step 016 does not allow without a new record, but the seam is what keeps that door from being welded shut.
path: 034. Signals meet at one replaceable collection point

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 One seam. Parts hand their signals to a single collection point; no part knows the address of a storage or visualisation backend. R2 A standard protocol. The handover uses a protocol the wider ecosystem speaks — neither parts nor backends tied to this organisation's tooling choices. R3 The observer is replaceable. Storage and visualisation tools behind the collection point can be changed, upgraded, or swapped without touching any part. R4 Instrumenting a part is cheap. A new part points at the collection point and exports; it gains the whole picture, not one backend's slice.
path: 034. Signals meet at one replaceable collection point

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Each part exports to its own backend R1: the backends become N dependencies instead of one seam; R3 with it — changing a backend is a change to every part. It can satisfy 016 perfectly, all data inside, which is exactly why it needs its own record to rule out. A seam speaking an in-house protocol R2: every backend behind the seam must be written or adapted for it, so the observer is not replaceable in practice (R3) and a new part needs custom wiring (R4). A sidecar or agent per part R2 and R4 kept; R1 strained — the picture is assembled from N agents whose configuration must agree — and a per-part mechanism to operate where one shared point suffices. Point at backends today, seam later Cheapest at the start; R3 fails at the moment of decision — the first backend change touches every part — and R1 defers into a migration whose cost grows with every part added before it. Do nothing (leave the seam implicit) The state this record corrects. Fails the organisation's: the next person to add a part or a backend would not know the seam exists, and wiring around it would not fail any check.
