path: 034. Signals meet at one replaceable collection point

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 034. Signals meet at one replaceable collection point

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• Changing an observation tool is a change behind the seam, not a change to the parts (R3).
  • A new part is instrumented once and gains every backend's view (R4).
  • The standard protocol keeps the door open to a future production arrangement without re-instrumentation — without committing to one.
path: 034. Signals meet at one replaceable collection point

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• The collection point is one more running part to start, keep healthy, and reason about when signals go missing: a failure at the seam blinds every backend at once.
  • The seam's standard protocol is the lowest common denominator, so a backend's richer features are reachable only behind it, never through the parts.
path: 034. Signals meet at one replaceable collection point

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• The browser-rendered part sending its signals to an address fixed in its own build is a deviation from this record's single seam until the address arrives through the deployment channel (018). The example app now takes its exporter URL from the fetched runtime config — the deviation is closed there; the vendored dashboard remains out of scope (030).
  • A deployment that names no collection point runs blind by choice — a gap to name rather than tolerate; how the collection point deploys in a customer's environment follows 016's boundary rule.
  • How long the signals the collection point holds are kept is a lifetime question owned by 025, not this record.
Why does a standard protocol matter if nothing ever exports?

Because the protocol is the cheap insurance. The picture lives inside (016) and no export is allowed without a new record — but an in-house seam protocol makes every future option a re-instrumentation project (R2, R3). The standard keeps the door unlocked at the cost of lowest-common-denominator features.
path: 034. Signals meet at one replaceable collection point

items.title: 035. Parts hand work to each other through a durable event log
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-07
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise
path: 035. Parts hand work to each other through a durable event log

items.title: Decision
items.text:
Business events — the record of what happened — flow between parts through a durable, replayable event log, and that log is the default way one part makes a fact available to others. A part may still answer a caller directly when a person is waiting; the log is where the shared record lives, not a copy of every request. A new part that needs an existing fact subscribes to the log rather than asking the part that produced it.

This decision was already in force before it was written down: the development arrangement starts the platform, the examples produce events to it and consume them from it, and a sink carries those events into storage. What this record adds is the rule itself — that the log is the default integration substrate and that joining the system is a subscription, not a new bridge between two parts.
path: 035. Parts hand work to each other through a durable event log

items.title: Context
items.text:
The system is made of parts that were built separately and must keep working together as they are added and removed. When one part learns something the business cares about, that fact has to reach the parts that act on it and the places that keep it. The question is how the fact travels.

The cheapest answer — the caller calls the next part directly — binds the two together: the caller must know the callee, reach it now, and be changed again when a new reader appears. As parts come and go, that binding becomes the cost of every change. A shared table is another answer, but it shows only the state right now, not the ordered record of what happened, so a part that starts late cannot catch up on what it missed.

The system is also meant to run whole on one machine and be validated against real services, so whatever carries the facts must run there too, not only in a hosted deployment. And because the examples are how the organisation teaches, the way facts move in an example is the way the next system will move them.

The decision to make is what carries the shared record of what happened, and what a part must do to make a fact available or to consume one.
path: 035. Parts hand work to each other through a durable event log

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

  • R1 — Producer and consumer are not tied together in time or knowledge. A part can make a fact available without knowing which parts will use it or whether they are running now.
  • R2 — The record is durable and replayable. A part that starts later, or recovers from a stop, can catch up on what it missed rather than seeing only the state that remains.
  • R3 — One fact can reach many users without the producer changing. Adding a reader does not rewrite the writer.
  • R4 — Joining the system is a subscription, not a bridge. A new part that needs an existing fact consumes it rather than forcing new wiring into the part that produced it.
  • R5 — The arrangement runs where the system is built and validated. The event path is live on one machine and in the pipeline, not only in a hosted deployment.
  • R6 — Removing a part does not strand what it produced or consumed. The record outlives the parts that used it.
  • R7 — A person waiting is served directly. The log carries the shared record of what happened; it does not replace the immediate answer an interactive surface needs.
path: 035. Parts hand work to each other through a durable event log

items.title: Alternatives
items.text:
• Direct calls between parts only. Each part calls the next by name. It fails R1 — the caller must know and reach the callee now — R3, because a new reader means changing the writer, and R4, because every new consumer is new wiring in an existing part.
  • A shared store as the medium. Parts meet by reading and writing common tables. It fails R2: a table shows the current state, not the ordered record of what happened, so a late or recovered part cannot replay what it missed; and it ties every reader to one shape at once.
  • Ad hoc integration per pair. Each connection is built when a need appears. It fails R4 and R6 — the wiring is bespoke and the record is whatever the pair privately agreed, so removing a part can strand it.
  • Do nothing (each part chooses). It costs nothing today and lets the cheapest local answer win; it fails R1 and R4 by default, because the default becomes a direct call and joining the system means touching parts that already work.
path: 035. Parts hand work to each other through a durable event log

items.title: Tradeoffs
items.text:
• Positive: parts are decoupled in time and in what they must know of each other (R1, R4); one fact serves many users without rework (R3); a late or recovered part can catch up rather than guess (R2); a part removed leaves the record intact (R6).
  • Negative: the log is infrastructure to run and to understand, and it joins what a new joiner must learn; a fact reaches a reader a moment after it happens rather than instantly, so parts must tolerate brief lag; debugging "the fact has not arrived yet" is harder than debugging a call that failed loudly; and an example that skips the platform teaches the wrong shape.
  • Neutral / follow-ups: the guarantee a single stream gives is owned by the delivery-guarantee record (027), the naming of streams by the naming record (032), the compatibility of the events themselves by the shared-concept record (017), and the canonical shape of the concept an event carries by the domain-model record (004); the platform running on one machine and in the pipeline is the arrangement the whole-system record already requires (006). The placeholder pages on data pipelines and on integration methods under the architecture section remain headings until written from this answer; where a part integrates by a direct call today rather than joining the log, that is a named deviation to be either justified or brought in line.
path: 035. Parts hand work to each other through a durable event log

items.title: 036. The delivery plane is a named exception to the data boundary
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-07
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

The data boundary protects the running system without exception. The delivery plane may cross it only at named, recorded points: each outside service is a named entry, and a new exit is a new record, not a pipeline edit.
path: 036. The delivery plane is a named exception to the data boundary

items.title: Decision
items.text:
The boundary protects the running system; the delivery plane crosses at named points. The running system and its operational picture stay inside the boundary without exception. The delivery plane — the pipeline that validates and releases the system — may use outside services, and each is a named entry: the tool, the kind of data it receives, and why the system's own tools do not answer. A delivery tool not on the list may not receive data from the pipeline, and a new entry is a new record, not a pipeline edit.

This decision was in force before it was written down: the pipeline sends interface snapshots of the user interface to a visual-review service and source metadata to a hosted code-analysis service, while the running system and its traces, metrics, and logs have never left. What this record adds is the principle that makes those two uses deliberate rather than contradictory.
path: 036. The delivery plane is a named exception to the data boundary

items.title: Context
items.text:
The system keeps its operational picture inside its own boundary (016): no trace, metric, or log reaches an outside service, so the system runs and is legible wherever it runs, including offline and where data may not leave. That rule was written as a rule about the system, and it still holds without exception.

The pipeline is a different activity. It answers questions about the code and interface before they ship — does this change alter a screen a customer relies on, does this source introduce a known flaw — and for those the organisation has chosen hosted services, because the comparison they provide (against every previous screen, against a continuously updated catalogue of known flaws) is not something the system's own tools maintain. Those services receive data: pictures of interfaces, metadata about source.

The two arrangements sit close enough to be confused for each other. A reader of the boundary rule alone would expect the pipeline to send nothing anywhere; a reader of the pipeline alone would expect the boundary to be a preference. Neither is true, and the ambiguity is the risk: the next delivery tool can be added by anyone, and without a stated rule there is no way to tell a considered exception from a leak.

Why a named exception, not a weakened rule

Deleting the boundary for the pipeline, or pretending the pipeline sends nothing, both destroy the ability to say which is which. A named exception keeps the rule absolute — the system sends nothing out — and puts the one sending activity on a list where a reviewer can see it. The record that names an exception is what makes "we checked" answerable.
path: 036. The delivery plane is a named exception to the data boundary

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 The boundary is stated by data class, not by tool. Which data may never leave and which the delivery plane may send, from the rule itself — no tool list needed. R2 The running system is never the exception. No deployed part sends anything outside; the exception belongs to the pipeline alone. R3 Operational data is never the exception. Traces, metrics, and logs stay inside in every activity, delivery included. R4 Every crossing is named. Per outside service: the tool, the data kind, the reason the system's tools don't suffice. R5 Crossing is a recorded act. A new data-receiving delivery service means a new record; a pipeline change alone cannot open an exit. R6 The system still runs offline. The exception creates no dependency a machine without network access would miss.
path: 036. The delivery plane is a named exception to the data boundary

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails No exceptions: boundary covers everything Clean and absolute; fails R4's purpose in the other direction — the pipeline already uses hosted comparison services, so the rule is either false on paper or forces removing tools whose value the organisation chose to keep. A rule the working pipeline quietly violates teaches readers to ignore it. Boundary as a preference, per tool R1 and R5: with no stated principle, every addition is a judgement call, and the difference between a considered exception and an accident is whoever notices. Supersede the boundary entirely R2 and R3 outright: the system runs offline and in restricted environments because the boundary holds for the running system — dissolving it to legitimise two pipeline services trades portability for convenience. Self-host replacements for both Keeps every byte inside; fails the reason the services are used: the value is the comparison against history and a maintained external catalogue, and a self-hosted copy of that standing is upkeep the organisation has not chosen to operate. Do nothing (leave the ambiguity) Free today; R1 and R5 by leaving the boundary readable two ways — the state in which an unlisted exit gets added without anyone deciding anything.
path: 036. The delivery plane is a named exception to the data boundary

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 036. The delivery plane is a named exception to the data boundary

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• The boundary rule can be stated without asterisks, because the exception is a separate, smaller rule (R1).
  • The running system keeps every benefit of the boundary — offline, restricted, customer environments (R2, R3, R6).
  • The next exit is a decision with a paper trail, not a pull request nobody read (R5).
path: 036. The delivery plane is a named exception to the data boundary

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• Two rules where a reader hoped for one, and the line between "delivery plane" and "system" must be held in every future review.
  • Each named service is a dependency the pipeline can fail on and a recipient the organisation must trust with the data class it receives.
  • The exception invites pressure to widen it, which R5 exists to slow down.
path: 036. The delivery plane is a named exception to the data boundary

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• The current entries: the visual-review service (receives interface snapshots) and the hosted code-analysis service (receives source metadata). A tool that begins receiving more than its entry states has opened an unrecorded exit — each entry's data kind is a standing obligation.
  • Whether the gate enforces those services' findings is a question the gate and causation records answer (014, 015).
  • This record narrows nothing about the boundary itself — 016's rule stands as written, and any change to it is a supersession, not an edit.
Why not just keep every byte inside?

Because the hosted services sell comparison, not storage: every previous screen, a continuously updated flaw catalogue. Self-hosting that standing is an upkeep the organisation has declined (the alternatives table), and banning them would make the boundary rule false on paper — a rule the working pipeline violates without anyone noticing (the first alternative). Naming the two exits is what keeps the rule both true and absolute where it counts.
path: 036. The delivery plane is a named exception to the data boundary

items.title: 037. The system itself promises nothing about staying up
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-07
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

Availability is not a property the system carries — it is a property the adopting deployment builds around it. The system promises no uptime of its own: it must not fake availability, and it must not prevent it.
path: 037. The system itself promises nothing about staying up

items.title: Decision
items.text:
Availability belongs to the deployment, not the system. The system promises no uptime of its own, and the rule has two halves: it must not fake availability — no page, guide, or example may claim resilience the arrangement does not provide — and it must not prevent availability — a part holds no private state that would pin it to one instance, and state that must exist lives in named stores a deployment can protect.

What the system does promise about loss and downtime is the recovery promise, owned by 026 — not a prevention promise.

This decision was in force before it was written down: every part runs as an instance a deployment can multiply, the state the system keeps sits in stores a deployment can name and protect, and nothing claims an uptime no mechanism backs. What this record adds is the posture in words, so that the absence of a cluster reads as a decision rather than an omission.
path: 037. The system itself promises nothing about staying up

items.title: Context
items.text:
People who meet the system ask, directly or by implication, how safe it is to depend on: what happens when a machine fails, whether a service can be lost for an hour, whether data survives.

The honest answer today is that the system, as built, provides no protection of its own — every part runs as a single instance, and the arrangement is deliberately small. That answer is reasonable for what the system is: an arrangement validated whole on one machine (006), meant to be deployed inside infrastructure the adopting organisation already operates.

The risk is not the smallness; it is the ambiguity around it:

  • A reader who finds guidance about replicating services can mistake advice to a future deployment for a property of the system.
  • A reader who finds no statement at all can assume protection exists and build on it.
  • A reviewer of the next design can read the missing cluster as an oversight and add machinery nobody asked for.

Each of these costs more than the missing sentence. The forces pull two ways: stating "no availability promise" plainly is honest but can be read as permission to ignore resilience; promising resilience the system does not have is worse — it moves the failure from the machine to the trust.
path: 037. The system itself promises nothing about staying up

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 The posture is stated, not inferred. "Is this resilient?" is answered in a record, not in the silence between a single-instance arrangement and a replication tip. R2 No claim without a mechanism. No document, guide, or example presents protection the system does not provide. R3 Nothing quietly prevents protection. A part can run in more than one instance, or be replaced while down, without losing the thread — no private state only it can recover. R4 State is enumerable. The state the system keeps lives in stores a person can list — what makes a deployment's protection decisions, and 026's promises, possible. R5 The development arrangement stays honest about itself. One instance of everything on one machine is a decision about where the system is built and validated, not a claim it can't run otherwise. R6 Advice to a deployment is marked as advice. Guidance about replicating or protecting services reads as a recommendation to whoever deploys, not a property of what is deployed.
path: 037. The system itself promises nothing about staying up

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Promise availability now: cluster everything R5 and the arrangement the whole-system record requires (006) — a cluster cannot be the daily development environment. It buys prevention the organisation has not asked for, at a price every run pays. Say nothing (the status quo) R1 by definition; R2 by omission: silence is where an unbacked claim gets read in, and where the missing cluster gets "fixed" by someone who never saw the decision. Per-part availability tiers R6's purpose at this scale: with one team and one arrangement, a catalogue of tiers is upkeep answering a question nobody has yet asked differently for two parts. Fold the question into recovery alone "We don't prevent, we recover" is half the answer, recorded in 026. R3: recovery of a store says nothing about whether a part can be multiplied or replaced — the prevention half. Do nothing Free today; fails every requirement the way the status quo does, by leaving the posture to be guessed.
path: 037. The system itself promises nothing about staying up

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 037. The system itself promises nothing about staying up

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• The missing cluster is a recorded decision, so reviewers protect it instead of "fixing" it (R1, R2).
  • The deployment team gets an honest starting point: the list of stores to protect, and the knowledge that parts can be multiplied (R3, R4).
  • The development arrangement is freed from being read as a production topology (R5).
path: 037. The system itself promises nothing about staying up

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• The system cannot win a requirement that demands built-in uptime, and the record says so plainly.
  • "The deployment owns it" transfers risk to a decision the adopting organisation has not always made yet — which makes this record a prerequisite for 024 to answer well.
  • R3 is a standing constraint on every future part: cheap per part, real in aggregate.
path: 037. The system itself promises nothing about staying up

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• The placeholder page on high availability under the architecture section remains a heading until written from this answer — as advice to a deployment, per R6, and the replication advice in the design guidance should be marked as such.
  • The recovery promise this record points at is itself Proposed (026): until it is accepted, the system promises neither prevention nor recovery, and that gap is stated here rather than papered over.
  • A part that begins holding private state a restart cannot recover is a deviation from R3 that belongs in this record's follow-ups until removed.
Isn't 'no availability promise' permission to ignore resilience?

It reads that way, and that reading is the record's named risk — R6 marks deployment guidance as advice precisely so the honest answer is not a shrug, and R3 makes the system enable resilience even while not promising it. What the system refuses is the unbacked claim: a promise with no mechanism moves the failure from the machine to the trust.
path: 037. The system itself promises nothing about staying up

items.title: 038. What a person may do is decided in one place, apart from who they are
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-07; accepted 2026-11-01
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

Accepted with increment 6.2c, as its acceptance trigger set (swept 2026-10-19): with 6.2a to 6.2c the server's authorizer answers every endpoint the server serves, as Atlas's checks do. The named mechanism is DD-300: four roles of the server's client in the identity provider, and what each grants is fixed in the server's authorization module. The spine holds both the mechanism and the roles, in the dev realm and in the cluster's.

The answer to "what is this person allowed to do?" lives in one named place, apart from the answer to "who is this person?". Surfaces ask and act; they do not invent permission rules in code.
path: 038. What a person may do is decided in one place, apart from who they are

items.title: Decision
items.text:
One authorizer, consulted not embedded. The answer to "what is this person allowed to do?" is held and enforced in one named place, deliberately apart from the answer to "who is this person?" (007). Surfaces ask that place and act on the answer; they do not invent their own rules in code.

Until this record was accepted, every authenticated person could do everything on every surface, and that was a stated condition, not a security property. The answer now lives in the identity provider's role assignments, read by one authorizer in the server (access management).
path: 038. What a person may do is decided in one place, apart from who they are

items.title: Context
items.text:
The system already knows who a person is: one identity provider admits people and every surface verifies what it issues, so no surface keeps its own account list. That answers admission; it does not answer permission. Today, once a person is admitted anywhere, they are admitted everywhere: the screens, the APIs behind them, and the operational tooling act on the verified identity and nothing else.

For the system as it stands — an arrangement being validated, with examples that demonstrate the shape — that is workable, and pretending otherwise would be false. But the system is meant to be deployed into environments that keep business data, and there "why could this person change that?" has to have an answer.

If nobody decides, the arrangement that exists is accidental: the first feature that needs a restriction grows a private check, the second grows a different one, and permission — the one security property auditors ask about most directly — becomes folklore scattered through surface code.

The forces are the same ones that settled identity: several surfaces, one truth, revocation that takes effect everywhere at once. Permission inherits them and adds one: a rule inside a surface can only change by releasing that surface, while the business reason for the rule changes on its own schedule.
path: 038. What a person may do is decided in one place, apart from who they are

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 One answer about permission. One authoritative statement of what each person or role may do; no private surface rules. R2 Revocation is one action. Withdrawing an allowance withdraws it at every surface, without releasing those surfaces. R3 Surfaces ask, then act. Enforcement consults the decided answer; the security-critical judgement is written, reviewed, and patched once. R4 The answer is auditable. "Who could do X, and when?" answered from the arrangement's records, not a code survey. R5 Permission runs where validation runs. The restricted path is live on one machine and in the pipeline, exercised routinely. R6 Cheap to keep true. A new surface or action joins the decided arrangement; the default is the shared answer, not a private check.
path: 038. What a person may do is decided in one place, apart from who they are

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Permission inside each surface R1: the truth is wherever the last check was written. R2: withdrawal is a release per surface. R4: the audit is a code survey. Permission at the network edge only R3 for anything the edge can't see — an event consumed directly, a call between parts. R4: the edge knows what was attempted, not what the business action meant. Role names baked into surface code Familiar and quick; R2 and R3: the meaning of a role is distributed across every release, and changing what a role may do is a code change everywhere at once. Defer permission entirely (status quo) Honest for a system with no business data yet. R1: the question is unowned. R6: the first urgent restriction is a bespoke check under time pressure — the arrangement every later one copies. Do nothing, hope the deployment adds it R5: a permission path that exists only in a deployment is a path no earlier run has exercised.
path: 038. What a person may do is decided in one place, apart from who they are

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 038. What a person may do is decided in one place, apart from who they are

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• Permission questions have one address (R1, R4); withdrawal is one act, not a release checklist (R2).
  • Surfaces stay thin, as identity made them thin.
  • The restricted path is exercised where every other security path is exercised (R5).
path: 038. What a person may do is decided in one place, apart from who they are

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• One more decision point in the request path, with its own failure mode to design for: what a surface does when the permission answer is unreachable is a question this record must eventually answer.
  • The arrangement is one more part to run locally and in the pipeline.
  • Naming roles is a business act that is wrong sometimes, so the arrangement must make being wrong cheap to fix.
path: 038. What a person may do is decided in one place, apart from who they are

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• The identity arrangement it sits beside is accepted (007) and stays re-opened-free: admission and permission remain separate answers even if one product holds both. The access-management placeholder page stays a heading until this record is accepted and written from its answer.
  • Machine identity for part-to-part calls belongs to 013, not here.
  • On acceptance, the named mechanism must exist in the spine (the parts that always stay, 002) before the status changes.
What if the authorizer is unreachable — fail open or closed?

Failing open would make availability the tiebreaker on every security question; this record's posture (037) refuses promises it can't keep in either direction. The posture it takes is the obligation: the behaviour is a named design decision at the seam, not an accident of timeout handling.

Answered on acceptance: closed. The roles travel in the access token the identity provider signs, and the server reads them in-process (DD-300), so there is no separate authorizer to lose. When the identity provider is unreachable no new token is issued, and a request without a valid token is refused. The price is R2's timing: withdrawing a role takes effect when the user's current access token expires, at most the realm's access-token lifespan (15 minutes on clusters).
path: 038. What a person may do is decided in one place, apart from who they are

items.title: 039. Data is protected where it travels and where it rests
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-10
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

Data is protected on the wire between parts and at rest in the stores — both declared, configured, checkable arrangements. Protection is the default, and every relaxation of it is named.
path: 039. Data is protected where it travels and where it rests

items.title: Decision
items.text:
Protection is a declared posture, in two places. Data is protected on the wire between parts and at rest in the stores it keeps. Both are declared arrangements — named, configured, and checkable — not properties assumed from the environment.

The mechanisms below exist in the development arrangement and in CI/E2E: a local certificate authority issues per-service certificates (nx certgen, each project's certs/), every store and service-to-service path verifies them, and the one named relaxation is the plaintext Keycloak browser listener of the local development arrangement.
path: 039. Data is protected where it travels and where it rests

items.title: Context
items.text:
The system moves data between parts — a browser to a service, a service to its store — and keeps data in stores: the search store, the operational signals. Protection has two costs, and they are asymmetric: it costs real work per run — certificates, trust, rotation, local tooling — and its absence costs a lump sum that arrives all at once, in an environment where it was assumed.

For the development arrangement, unprotected local paths are deliberate and cheap: everything runs on one machine, the paths never leave it, and certificate tax on every run protects a wire nobody can read (006 is right to keep the local arrangement simple).

The problem is what the arrangement teaches and what it ships. The examples are the taught path (009) — a part wired without protection in an example is wired without protection in the next system built from it. And the system is meant to be deployed into environments that keep business data, where both protections are usually not optional: carried between machines someone else operates, stored on media someone else owns.

The secrets record (008) already decided the credentials never exist in the clear; the data those credentials protect had no equivalent decision.
path: 039. Data is protected where it travels and where it rests

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 The posture is stated per place. What is protected, where required, where deliberately relaxed — never inferred from a localhost URL. R2 Protection is configured, not assumed. Where required, a mechanism enforces it and a reviewer sees the configuration; "the network is trusted" is not an arrangement. R3 The taught path matches the required path. An example shows the protected shape; an example running unprotected because it runs on one machine says so visibly. R4 Relaxation is local and named. Development may run unprotected and says so; an unprotected path outside development is a defect, not a default. R5 The check is cheap. Whether a path or store is protected is answered from configuration, not by probing a running system. R6 New parts inherit the posture. A new connection or store starts inside the declared arrangement.
path: 039. Data is protected where it travels and where it rests

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Protect everything, always, including local runs The arrangement the whole-system record requires (006) in its cheapest form: every run pays certificate setup to protect a wire that never leaves the machine — and the friction teaches people to disable the protection everywhere it matters. Protect nothing, let the deployment add it R3 and R6: the taught path stays unprotected, so the deployment inherits an unprotected shape and discovers the gap in production. R2: the deployment's protection is then nobody's configuration in this system. Protect only the browser-facing edge Familiar, since browsers insist. R1: the paths inside the system — service to store — are exactly the ones a deployed environment crosses machine boundaries on, and they stay declared by silence. Defer entirely (status quo) R1: the posture is guessed from localhost URLs. R3: the unprotected shape is taught as the normal one. Do nothing Free today; every requirement failed by the same silence — the current state described as a choice.
path: 039. Data is protected where it travels and where it rests

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 039. Data is protected where it travels and where it rests

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• The development arrangement keeps its cheap local paths with the relaxation written down instead of implied (R4).
  • The taught path shows the protected shape without dragging certificates into every run (R3).
  • A deployment gets a declared starting point: which paths must be protected and where the switches live (R2, R5).
path: 039. Data is protected where it travels and where it rests

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• Two postures (required, deliberately relaxed) are more to state and review than one absolute rule, and the line is a standing review question.
  • Protection has upkeep the system did not have — trust, rotation, expiry — and an expired certificate fails loudly at the worst moment.
  • Declaring development unprotected is itself an exposure a reader may copy if R4's visibility is not kept.
path: 039. Data is protected where it travels and where it rests

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• The credential rule it complements is accepted (008) — that record protects the keys to the data; this one protects the data itself. The identity of the parts on those paths is 013's: who may speak, not whether the words are private.
  • The operational signals' lifetime inside the protected stores is owned by 025.
  • The event-platform paths this record's first implementation listed (broker, registry, connectors) left with the streaming slice (050). The posture stands for the paths the catalogue keeps; the mechanisms that make it checkable are in TLS Certificates.
path: 039. Data is protected where it travels and where it rests

items.title: 040. The system raises its hand when it is broken
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Date: 2026-10-07
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

Acceptance trigger (swept 2026-10-19): increment 6.4 names the conditions, the destinations, and the silence trigger as alert rules in the observability stack; accepted in that pull request, recorded in the observability tree as it fills.

A condition that matters to the business has a named trigger and a named destination: the system notices and tells someone, without that person watching a screen. Collected signals nobody examines are a blind spot with extra steps.
path: 040. The system raises its hand when it is broken

items.title: Decision
items.text: Noticing is an arrangement, not a habit. A condition that matters to the business has a named trigger and a named destination: the system notices it and tells someone, without that person watching a screen. Signals collected but never examined are treated as a blind spot with extra steps, and a condition nobody is told about is a defect of the arrangement, not bad luck.
path: 040. The system raises its hand when it is broken

items.title: Context
items.text:
The system already produces its own picture and gathers it in one place: traces, metrics, and logs from every part meet at a collection point the system runs itself (016, 034). That arrangement made the picture available wherever the system runs. It says nothing about anyone looking.

Today nobody is told anything. The collection point holds the signals and a person reads them when they already suspect something — so the system's failures are discovered by whoever notices a symptom, usually a person outside the system, after the fact. The collection point's own storage can fill, a part can stop emitting and the picture simply goes quiet, and neither event announces itself.

The tension is between noticing and noise: a trigger for everything trains people to ignore triggers, and an ignored trigger is worse than none because it carries a false promise.

The tension is sharper here than in a typical deployment because the boundary rule (016) keeps the whole picture inside: there is no hosted service with alerting switched on by default, so noticing a failure is either a mechanism the organisation builds itself, or nobody does it.

And the availability posture (037) makes this record the system's only honest answer to "how would you know?" — the system promises no prevention, so detection is what remains.
path: 040. The system raises its hand when it is broken

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 Conditions are named, not improvised. The conditions worth announcing are written where a reviewer can see them; a trigger exists because someone chose it. R2 Every trigger has a destination. Who is told and how; a trigger that reaches nobody is a log line with a siren on. R3 Silence is itself a condition. A part that stops emitting, or a collection point that stops receiving, is a named trigger — the picture going quiet is an event. R4 Triggers stay worth reading. A condition that fires without action is revised or removed; the arrangement is graded by whether its announcements still mean something. R5 The mechanism lives inside the boundary. Noticing uses the signals the collection point already holds; nothing outside that the boundary forbids. R6 The path is exercised where validation runs. A trigger can be demonstrated to fire locally or in the pipeline; a trigger nobody has seen fire is decoration. R7 Cheap to keep true. A new part inherits the basic triggers — it is emitting, it is reachable — rather than arriving mute.
path: 040. The system raises its hand when it is broken

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Dashboards only (status quo) The picture exists for whoever looks. R2 and R3 by definition: nothing is announced, and the picture going quiet is precisely what a dashboard cannot show you. Alert on everything measurable R4: a stream nobody triages becomes wallpaper, and the wallpaper hides the one announcement that mattered. Watch the platform, not the conditions R1 for the business: a service can be healthy on every gauge and wrong in every answer — the conditions the business cares about are answers, not gauges. Rely on users to report The cheapest detector ever built. R2's purpose: the first informed person is the affected customer. R3: a system quiet enough to be broken quietly produces no complaints worth trusting. A hosted alerting service Mature and low-upkeep; R5: the raw material of noticing is the operational picture, and the boundary keeps that inside (016) — a hosted alert would ship the evidence out to announce it. Do nothing Free today; fails every requirement the way the status quo does, and leaves the availability posture (037) with no detection to stand on.
path: 040. The system raises its hand when it is broken

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 040. The system raises its hand when it is broken

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• Failures announce themselves instead of being excavated (R1, R2).
  • The blind spot of a quiet part or a full store closes (R3).
  • The boundary holds — noticing happens on the picture the system already keeps (R5).
  • The incident path has something to start from, which the incident-response question needs before it can be answered at all.
path: 040. The system raises its hand when it is broken

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• Triggers are upkeep: each one a condition to tune, a destination to keep current, a false alarm to learn from.
  • The first honest set of triggers is wrong in both directions until it is exercised.
  • Naming a destination for every trigger forces a question the organisation has not answered — who is told at what hour — which belongs to the incident record but cannot be dodged here.
path: 040. The system raises its hand when it is broken

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• This record is Proposed because the decision has not been made: the collection point holds the signals and no trigger reads them. The alerting placeholder page stays a heading until acceptance writes it from this answer.
  • What a person does after the hand is raised is the incident record's question (041), and that record leans on this one for the moment the incident begins.
  • The thresholds and numbers belong to whoever accepts this record and must be named at acceptance, not deferred.
  • A part that emits nothing is a deviation the observability record already names (016): an uninstrumented part cannot raise its hand, and this record inherits that blind spot until each part is instrumented or excused in writing.
Why is silence a trigger — isn't quiet normal?

Quiet is normal; unexplained quiet is the failure. A part that stops emitting and a collection point that stops receiving make the picture look healthy-by-absence (R3) — the one failure mode where "nothing to report" is indistinguishable from "no way to report." A heartbeat turns that ambiguity into an event.
path: 040. The system raises its hand when it is broken

items.title: 041. A failure of the running system has an owner and a rehearsed path
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-07
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

Accepted 2026-10-19: the owner of the response is the maintainers team; the path from noticing to closing, the rehearsed steps, and the incident record live in Operations Ownership. R4 holds today — the responder reads the system's own picture in the dev observability stack (ADRs 016, 034). Named gap: the detection half is the alerting arrangement of 040, scheduled with increment 6.4; the first rehearsal is scheduled.

When the running system fails, a named owner follows a written, rehearsed path. "Whoever notices" is not an owner, and an unwalked path is a paragraph.
path: 041. A failure of the running system has an owner and a rehearsed path

items.title: Decision
items.text:
A named owner, a written path, a rehearsal behind both. When the running system fails, the response follows a named path with a named owner: someone is answerable for deciding, someone for acting, and the steps — who is told, what is tried, when it escalates, what is written down afterwards — are written and rehearsed rather than improvised by whoever is nearest.

Before this record, the system had no incident path at all, and the owner of a failure became whoever happened to notice it — a default, not a decision.
path: 041. A failure of the running system has an owner and a rehearsed path

items.title: Context
items.text:
The system is built to be handed over: the records explain the decisions, the examples teach the shape, the development arrangement runs the whole thing on one machine. A failure response is the same kind of asset. When something breaks in an environment that matters, the cost of the failure is dominated by the hours around it — who was told, who decided, what was tried in what order, what was learned afterwards — and those hours are cheap only when the path was walked before.

The organisation already conceded this principle once, for credentials: secret handling has a named owner and a rehearsed path, because a lost key at midnight is not the moment to invent a process (028). The running system has no equivalent. Today's implicit path — whoever notices acts, whoever acts is answerable, the lessons leave with the person who learned them — has a name in every post-incident review ever written.

Two properties of this system sharpen the question:

  • The boundary (016) puts the evidence for any investigation inside the system, so the responder must read the system's own picture — an incident path that assumes a vendor's support line would be a fiction here.
  • The availability posture (037) says the system prevents nothing on its own: failures happen, and the honest answer to "what then?" is the path this record decides. The detection half — how anyone learns something is wrong — is owned by 040; this record starts where that one ends.
path: 041. A failure of the running system has an owner and a rehearsed path

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 An owner exists before the incident. One named role answers for deciding, escalating, closing. "Whoever is available" is the absence of an owner, not a kind of one. R2 The path is written. First signal to all-clear: who is told, in what order, what may be tried without asking, when it escalates, who says it is over. R3 The path is rehearsed. A path nobody has walked is a paragraph; practising it is on the schedule the rehearsal decays at, at worst. R4 The evidence is reachable by the responder. The responder reads the system's own picture without provisioning anything the boundary forbids. R5 Every incident leaves a record. What happened, what was done, what changes — where a future responder, or the next audit, can read it. R6 Learning closes the loop. A lesson that should become a rule or trigger becomes one — into alerting, recovery, or a new record — rather than resting in a file. R7 Cheap enough to survive. The path fits one small organisation: rehearsing is hours per year, not a department.
path: 041. A failure of the running system has an owner and a rehearsed path

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Whoever notices owns it (status quo) R1 by definition; R2: the path is invented at the worst moment; R5: the record of the incident is the chat log of whoever was paged. A formal incident-management process, imported whole ITIL-scale roles, severity matrices, war rooms. R7 at this scale: a process sized for a department goes unused by a team, and an unused process teaches the team to ignore process. Ad-hoc escalation by seniority Everyone knows who to call. R1: the owner is a person, not a role, and people leave. R3: a path carried in heads is unrehearsed by definition. Defer until the first real incident R3 outright: the first walk of an unrehearsed path is the incident itself, paid for by the people affected. R6: the lessons of that first incident are gathered by the exhausted people who lived it, if at all. Do nothing Free today; every requirement failed by the same silence — the current state described as a choice.
path: 041. A failure of the running system has an owner and a rehearsed path

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 041. A failure of the running system has an owner and a rehearsed path

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• A failure has an address before it happens (R1).
  • The hours around an incident shrink because the path is known and walked (R2, R3).
  • The organisation accumulates a written memory of its own failures (R5), and each incident makes the arrangement better instead of just over (R6).
path: 041. A failure of the running system has an owner and a rehearsed path

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• Naming an owner makes that role a single point unless backup is named too — the same hazard the secret-handling record accepts and manages (028).
  • Rehearsal is real time spent on a disaster hoped against.
  • A written path invites mechanical following when the incident does not match it — the owner's judgement must be trusted to override.
path: 041. A failure of the running system has an owner and a rehearsed path

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• This record leans on the alerting record (040) for the moment an incident begins — and that record is itself Proposed, so today the system neither raises its hand nor answers when one is raised.
  • The recovery half of a severe incident — bringing the system back from a named snapshot — is owned by 026; this record is the path that invokes it.
  • The owner role named here and the secret-handling owner (028) may be the same role or must at least know each other — decided at acceptance of both.
  • The numbers — rehearsal cadence, escalation times — belong to whoever accepts this record and must be named then, not deferred.
Why rehearse when the owner is one small team?

Because the path's value is exactly its unexercised state: nobody on the team walks an incident path weekly, so the only moments of practice are the rehearsal and the incident (R3). An unpractised path decays at staff turnover — a step naming a tool or person that has moved on is a paragraph, not a path.
path: 041. A failure of the running system has an owner and a rehearsed path

items.title: 042. Every dataset has an owner who answers for it
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Date: 2026-10-07
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

Every dataset the system keeps has an owner — a named role that answers for its shape, lifetime, and quality. A dataset may be declared shared, but sharing is itself the ownership answer, with a named custodian.
path: 042. Every dataset has an owner who answers for it

items.title: Decision
items.text:
Every dataset has a name beside it. Every dataset the system keeps — a table, an index, a store of operational signals — has an owner: a named role that answers for its shape, its lifetime, and its quality, and whose approval a change to those needs. A dataset may be declared shared, but sharing is itself the ownership answer, recorded with a named custodian — not the absence of one.

Until this record is accepted, a dataset with more than one writer has no answer at all, and disagreements about it are settled by whoever edits first.
path: 042. Every dataset has an owner who answers for it

items.title: Context
items.text:
The system keeps data in places with different lives: business rows in stores, operational signals in their own stores. Each raises the same quiet question — who answers for this? — and today the answer is nowhere written.

The question stopped being theoretical the moment one store grew a second hand. The record's founding example — the database the API writes and the event sink also writes — travelled with the streaming slice (050), but the shape it exposed is permanent: one store, several hands, each shaped by a different part's needs. A change to what a row means is a change to what the other hand stores, and neither part's tests can see the other's assumption.

The founding example, and why the shape outlives it

The example — one database written by both an API and an event sink — arrived with the streaming slice and left with it (050). The lesson did not: any store with two writers has it. The catalogue's own audit writer and entity store meet the same shape when increment 3.5 lands, so the ownership question the record answers is not a leftover of the slice.

Two records meet at this gap and stop short of it:

  • The migration record (023) decides how a schema changes; it cannot decide who says yes.
  • The shared-concept record (004) decides a concept has one canonical definition; it does not decide who answers when two parts want the definition to bend.

The softer costs are real. A person asking "can we trust this number?" has no one to ask. A dataset nobody owns is a dataset nobody notices decaying, and its lifetime question (025) has no one to answer it in practice. When a dataset is retired, nobody can say what still reads it.

The force is not team size — even one team hands over: new joiners, agents working from the codebase, future reviewers all ask "who cares about this table?" and today the codebase does not say.
path: 042. Every dataset has an owner who answers for it

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 Every dataset has a name beside it. A named role answers for each; the list of datasets and owners stays small enough to stay true. R2 Sharing is a stated answer. Several writers means declared shared, with a named custodian who arbitrates shape. "Several writers, no answer" is not permitted. R3 The owner's say is defined. Shape, lifetime, or meaning changes require the owner's approval, named in the change — not consulted by folklore. R4 Ownership survives people. The owner is a role, not a person's memory; when the person changes, the answer does not. R5 The answer is findable. "Who owns this?" answered beside the dataset or in one short list, not by asking around. R6 Cheap to keep true. A new dataset arrives with its owner named in the change that creates it — one line, not a ceremony.
path: 042. Every dataset has an owner who answers for it

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Ownership by writer (status quo) R2 the moment a second writer appears — which has already happened. R3: two writers means two answers, and the one that wins is whoever ships first. Ownership by the whole team R1 in practice: everyone cares, so no one answers — a question about the data has no address, and R3's approval is a meeting instead of a decision. A data governance board R6 at this scale: a board for a handful of datasets is ceremony the first urgent change routes around, and a routed-around process is worse than none. Ownership by the schema's source of truth R2 directly: the shared store is precisely the case where two models meet. R5: the answer is a deduction from code, not a stated fact. Do nothing Free today. R1: the question goes unasked. Every later record that needs an owner — lifetime, quality, lineage, compliance — inherits the silence.
path: 042. Every dataset has an owner who answers for it

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 042. Every dataset has an owner who answers for it

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• Questions about data have an address (R1, R5).
  • The shared store's multi-writer problem gets an arbiter instead of a race (R2).
  • The lifetime and quality questions finally have someone to answer them — 025 assumes this record supplies.
  • A new joiner or agent learns who cares about a table without asking (R4, R5).
path: 042. Every dataset has an owner who answers for it

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• Ownership lines are upkeep: a dataset whose owner left is a lie waiting to be read, so R4 needs a real hand-over habit.
  • Naming an owner invites ownership to expand into style review and veto over everything; R3 must bound it to shape, lifetime, and meaning.
  • Declaring a dataset shared with a custodian still concentrates arbitration in one role — exercised visibly, or it decays into the status quo with extra paperwork.
path: 042. Every dataset has an owner who answers for it

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• The mechanism — where the dataset-and-owner list lives, how a change proves the owner's approval — must be named at acceptance, not deferred.
  • The division of labour: 023 decides how a schema changes and this record decides who says yes; 004 decides what a concept means and this record supplies the role that answers when meanings are contested; 025 needs an owner per kind of data to state its numbers, and this record is where that owner comes from.
  • The placeholder pages on data-governance roles and the data dictionary remain headings until acceptance; the lineage and compliance questions under the same section lean on this record's substrate and should not be framed before it.
Why is 'owned by the team' not good enough?

Because it dissolves exactly when a decision is needed (R1, R3). "The team cares" has no address to send a shape change to, no name to put on an approval, and no one who notices decay. The record allows shared datasets (R2) — what it forbids is a sharing answer with no custodian attached.
path: 042. Every dataset has an owner who answers for it

items.title: 043. AI-assisted review informs the two signatures; it does not replace them
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-08
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

Automated review is a welcome first pass on any change. Its findings follow the ordinary blocking rule; its approval is never one of the two human signatures, and dismissing a machine finding is a human act, recorded as one.
path: 043. AI-assisted review informs the two signatures

items.title: Decision
items.text:
The assistant reads first; the humans sign. Automated review — an assistant reading the diff and leaving findings — is a permitted and welcome first pass on any change, human- or agent-authored.

Its findings obey the ordinary rule: those about the change itself block when the gate (the shared set of checks every change must pass, 014) enforces them, and those about the state of the world are advisory evidence for the cadence review (015).

An automated review comment is never an approval: the two human signatures stand (044), and dismissing a machine finding is a human act, recorded as one.
path: 043. AI-assisted review informs the two signatures

items.title: Context
items.text:
A small team has little review time, and fast generation multiplies the volume of diff arriving at it.

The team already uses assistants to read diffs — the commit history carries the residue of applied review feedback — but an unstated practice drifts in the direction of least effort: first toward treating a machine's approval as the second signature, then toward dismissing its findings without reading them, then toward skipping the human review the machine seemed to make unnecessary.

Each drift has a known failure:

  • A machine cannot be accountable for a merged change (044), so an approval that is not a human's leaves R1 unanswered.
  • Machine findings include plausible mistakes, and a finding dismissed unread is a defect adopted with confidence.
  • Treating every machine finding as blocking would import the noise of the whole ecosystem into the merge gate — the exact failure the blocking rule exists to prevent (015) — and would train the team to bypass the review as they bypass a noisy gate.
path: 043. AI-assisted review informs the two signatures

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 The signatures stay human. Automated review may inform both signatures, satisfy neither; no workflow accepts a bot approval as the second pair of eyes. R2 Machine findings follow the blocking rule. A finding blocks only when the defined gate enforces it; a reviewer's judgement of a machine comment never changes what blocks. R3 Dismissal is a human act. Every rejected machine finding is dismissed by a named person, visible in the review — a wrong machine verdict cannot silently become a merged defect. R4 Volume does not lower the bar. The practice must hold when review volume is high; a practice that only works with a short queue is the first thing skipped under pressure. R5 Cheap to keep true. No new roles, queues, or dashboards; the practice rides the review surface the team already uses.
path: 043. AI-assisted review informs the two signatures

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails No automated review Passes R1 trivially, but fails the reason the practice exists: at generated volume, human review without a machine first pass becomes the bottleneck that squeezes understanding out of the second signature. Machine approval as the second signature Fails R1: a bot cannot explain the change in six months, cannot carry it in an incident, cannot be the accountable party — the same point 042 makes about ownership. Machine findings always block R2 and R4: machine review produces confident nonsense at a steady rate, and a gate that must be argued with is a gate that gets bypassed — the failure named in 015. Machine findings invisible (off the review) Findings go to a side channel. R3: dismissals happen off the record. R5: a second surface is a second thing to maintain, then ignore. Do nothing (status quo, unstated) The practice continues without a boundary. Fails R1 gradually: each relaxation is individually reasonable, and together they replace the second signature.
path: 043. AI-assisted review informs the two signatures

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 043. AI-assisted review informs the two signatures

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• The team keeps the capacity gain of a machine first pass without letting it redefine accountability (R1).
  • Machine findings arrive where humans already read, at no new ceremony (R5).
  • The dismissal rule turns each wrong machine verdict into visible evidence about the tool, rather than an invisible defect (R3).
path: 043. AI-assisted review informs the two signatures

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• Machine review consumes human attention to triage its findings, and at high false-positive rates the tax can exceed the saving — the response is to tune or drop the reviewer, never to relax R3.
  • The rule depends on reviewers actually reading machine comments: the same review-discipline dependency the instruction layer carries (022).
path: 043. AI-assisted review informs the two signatures

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• R1's force rests on the merge mechanism that enforces the two signatures (044); R3's dismissal habit on review discipline (022).
  • Whether machine findings should ever be promoted to blocking is a decision under 015, not this record.
If the bot finds the bug, why can't its approval count?

Because an approval is an assumption of accountability, and a bot can't carry one: it cannot explain the change in six months, own it in an incident, or answer for a dataset it blessed (R1, 042). The bot's finding is welcome — the human who reads it and signs is the mechanism.
path: 043. AI-assisted review informs the two signatures

items.title: 044. Every change carries two human signatures
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-08
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

Every change that merges carries two human signatures — the task owner and one reviewer — enforced by a mechanism that refuses the merge. An assistant may produce, test, and review a change; it signs nothing.
path: 044. Every change carries two human signatures

items.title: Decision
items.text:
Two signatures, both human. Every change that merges into the mainline carries the task owner — the person who asked for the change, who can explain it, and who states how far they verified it locally — and one reviewer, a second person who confirms independent understanding.

A tool signs nothing. An automated assistant may produce, test, and review a change, but accountability is carried by the team and cannot be offloaded to a tool.

The rule has an enforcement point. A mechanism refuses the merge without the second approval; the rule is not held by custom.
path: 044. Every change carries two human signatures

items.title: Context
items.text:
The repository is changed routinely by automated agents as well as by people, and the cost of producing a plausible diff has fallen sharply. The obligation attached to a change has not: the team must be able to own what it ships, and ownership requires understanding.

  • Understanding is no longer a side effect. Before fast generation, the author's understanding came free with writing the code by hand. Now a change can arrive working, gated, and reviewed by machines while nobody on the team fully understands it. The failure is quiet — it surfaces at the next incident, the next change to the same area, the next handover — and the delay is what makes it debt rather than a defect.
  • The oldest review rule needs teeth. The contributor guide has always required a second pair of eyes. That rule was written for a slower generator; what changes when code is produced quickly is how load-bearing it becomes, and a rule held only by custom is the first thing a fast queue erodes.
path: 044. Every change carries two human signatures

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 A human answers for every change. A named person can explain each merged change and carries it; "the assistant wrote it" is not an answer to "who owns this?". R2 Understanding is independent. At least one person besides the task owner reads the change for understanding before it merges; self-approval is not approval. R3 Verification is stated, not assumed. The task owner records how far they verified locally, so a reviewer knows whether "it works" means lint passed or the real system ran. R4 The rule has an enforcement point. A mechanism refuses the merge without the second signature — not a convention that erodes when delivery is late. R5 Cheap enough to keep. Two signatures on a typical change is minutes, not a ceremony; the rule must not push people to route around it. R6 Knowledge moves with review. The reviewer is chosen at least partly for who should learn the area, so review doubles as knowledge spread.
path: 044. Every change carries two human signatures

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails One signature (the status quo) R2: the gate checks form and behavior, not whether anyone understands; R6: knowledge concentrates in whoever prompted the change. Machine review is enough R1 and R2: a machine verdict is evidence, not accountability — the organisation still needs a person who can explain the change six months from now. Committee approval for agent changes R5, and it contradicts the no-privileged-path rule (022): risk follows blast radius, not the typist's identity, and a special lane trains the team to hide assistant involvement. Custom only R4: the first urgent merge that skips review establishes the exception, and at generated volume the exceptions become the rule silently. Do nothing R1, the first time a change breaks and nobody on the team can explain it.
path: 044. Every change carries two human signatures

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 044. Every change carries two human signatures

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• Every merged change has a human who can explain it (R1) and a second human who is starting to (R2, R6).
  • The verification statement makes the strength of "it works" visible at review time (R3).
  • The merge mechanism turns the oldest review rule in the guide into an enforcement point (R4) — what 017 asks of review-only conventions.
path: 044. Every change carries two human signatures

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• Two humans per change is the scarcest budget in a small team, and generation volume can make the second signature the bottleneck — the pressure is to approve quickly, which R6 mitigates only if reviewer selection stays deliberate.
  • Declaring the task owner adds one line of ceremony to every pull request.
  • The merge mechanism can be overridden by repository administrators, so it needs the same habit as the gate (the shared set of checks every change must pass, 014).
path: 044. Every change carries two human signatures

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• The mechanism that makes R4 true lives in the hosting platform's merge settings — an implementation detail of where the rule is enforced, not part of the decision. The pull request template carries the two signatures and the verification statement.
  • Assistant review is governed separately (043); the no-privileged-path rule is this record's neighbour, not its source (022); what the reviewer may rely on the gate for is decided by the blocking rule (015).
The owner understands the change — why is a second human needed?

The owner's understanding is exactly what generation makes unreliable: a change can arrive working and gated while nobody, including the owner, fully grasps it (R2). The second reader is the only independent check that understanding exists at all — and choosing that reader deliberately is how knowledge spreads instead of concentrating (R6).
path: 044. Every change carries two human signatures

items.title: 045. Conventions are borrowed before they are invented
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-08
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

Every convention is borrowed along a three-rung ladder — the framework's, then the community's, then a local rule — and each rung must be shown empty before the next. In-house dialects are the most expensive knowledge a codebase can hold.
path: 045. Conventions are borrowed before they are invented

items.title: Decision
items.text:
A ladder of three rungs. Every convention the organisation could write is borrowed first:

  1. The framework's conventions. When a technology slot is filled — a web framework, a frontend framework, a validation library — the default is the mainstream option whose conventions do the most work: the framework decides where code goes, how it is wired, and what is valid, so the organisation writes rules only where the framework is silent.
  2. The community's conventions. Where the framework is silent, adopt the settled habits of its ecosystem — naming, test layout, commit titles — rather than inventing.
  3. A local rule. Invention is permitted only where no framework or community convention covers the gap, and it names the empty rung it stands on.

New stacks ask the ladder first. A technology joins by recipe (021), and the recipe's first question is "which existing convention already covers this?", not "what shall we invent?". An organisation this size does not write a framework, or a dialect, to make a choice it can borrow.

Borrowing is load-bearing, not decorative. Framework majors are planned events, not routine updates (020), and a framework's defaults are adopted through the declared channel rather than trusted silently (018).
path: 045. Conventions are borrowed before they are invented

items.title: Context
items.text:
The repository spans several stacks maintained by one small, multi-disciplinary team, and it is changed routinely by automated agents as well as by people (022).

  • Invented rules cost attention forever. Every convention the organisation invents must be written down, taught to every new joiner, restated in the machine-facing instructions, checked in review, and re-learned by every agent session — forever, and per stack. Every borrowed convention is known by every new joiner who has worked in that ecosystem, and is the shape an assistant produces when nobody tells it otherwise.
  • The failure has a known shape. A feature-first choice leaves the framework's job half-done, the team finishes it privately — a directory layout, a wiring style, a settings story — and maintains a small framework nobody outside can read. That private dialect is the most expensive kind of knowledge in a codebase: it exists only in the heads of the people who wrote it, and it is exactly the knowledge an agent cannot pick up on its own.
  • The same reasoning applies below the framework level. A framework cannot settle every habit — commit titles, test naming and placement — and those gaps are where teams grow a house style. But most gaps already have a settled community answer, and a borrowed community convention carries the same assets as a borrowed framework convention.
  • The record must outlive the brands. Frameworks and libraries change while the business reasoning does not, so this record states the preference that governs how conventions are acquired — not which framework fills which slot today.
path: 045. Conventions are borrowed before they are invented

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 Structure arrives borrowed. The framework, then the community, supply the default answers for layout, wiring, validation, and everyday habits, so the written rule set stays small and covers only genuine local decisions. R2 Strangers read the code. A competent outsider — joiner, reviewer, or assistant — who knows the stack reads the code without learning a private dialect; understanding is a hiring and onboarding asset (003). R3 The convention is load-bearing on purpose. Upgrades are planned, defaults are validated through the declared channel, and the convention is not quietly worked around. R4 The choice stays replaceable. The preference is about properties, not brands; replacing a framework is a planned migration under 020, not a decision reversal. R5 New stacks join through the same gate. A technology that genuinely needs new ground enters by recipe (021) with its conventions documented beside it. R6 Invention is the last resort. A local convention is permitted only where no framework or community convention covers the gap; an invented rule that could have been borrowed is a defect of the same kind as a private dialect.
path: 045. Conventions are borrowed before they are invented

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Feature-first selection Choose the most capable framework. R1: capability-first choices are typically the least opinionated, and the unopinionated space is filled by an invented in-house dialect — the cost R1 exists to avoid. In-house framework Fails R2 by design: the dialect is private. R3: the team that builds a framework also has to operate, document, and staff it, which a small team pays for twice. Private house style Keep the frameworks, invent the open habits. R6 where a borrowed answer exists; R2 where the invented answer diverges from what joiners and assistants arrive knowing. A style guide is still a rule re-learned by every session. Maximal minimalism One language, one framework, nothing new (021 rejects this). R1 and R2 for the stacks it keeps; R5: it freezes the stack rather than expressing a preference about how new parts join. No stated preference Decide each slot ad hoc. R4: the absence of a rule is itself decided differently every time. R1: ad hoc selection drifts toward the familiar-but-thin option, and invented conventions return. Do nothing Keep the stack without recording why. R3: an unrecorded preference is argued again at every upgrade, and the first "just this once" exception starts the drift back to the private dialect.
path: 045. Conventions are borrowed before they are invented

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 045. Conventions are borrowed before they are invented

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• The written rule set stays small because the framework and its community carry the structure and the habits (R1, R6).
  • Onboarding and assistant-authored changes start from the stack's conventions instead of a local dialect (R2), which lightens the instruction layer (022).
  • Review spends attention on meaning because form is typical of the stack.
  • The preference is brand-independent, so it survives every migration (R4).
path: 045. Conventions are borrowed before they are invented

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• Mainstream conventions are not always the best conventions: the team inherits decisions it did not make, and escaping one — a framework fighting a requirement — costs more than never adopting it.
  • Community conventions are softer than framework ones: they shift, and two communities can disagree, so R6's "no convention covers this" needs judgement at the edges — and a settled habit the team dislikes must be swallowed or consciously opted out of, not silently diverged from.
  • The commitment is real: planned majors (020) and declared-channel settings (018) are obligations, not decorations.
  • "Mainstream" narrows the field in a way that must be re-examined when a genuinely better convention matures.
path: 045. Conventions are borrowed before they are invented

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• Which framework fills which slot today is an implementation note and deliberately absent from this record — it belongs in the project documentation that describes each stack (003).
  • The enforcement point is the recipe review that every new technology passes through (021).
Why is a private style guide a defect?

Because every rule in it is paid for forever: written down, taught, restated to agents, and checked in review, while a borrowed rule arrives free with the ecosystem. A house style guide is a dialect with documentation — and a dialect is precisely what joiners and agents cannot pick up on their own (R2, R6).
path: 045. Conventions are borrowed before they are invented

items.title: 046. The catalogue keeps its public contract while its implementation is replaced
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-09
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

The metadata catalogue's implementation is being replaced; what users and integrations see is not. The same HTTP interface, the same shapes and error codes, the same screens — an unnamed difference is a defect, a named one a recorded deviation.
path: 046. The catalogue keeps its public contract

items.title: Decision
items.text:
The contract is frozen; the implementation moves. The catalogue's implementation is replaced without changing what its users and integrations see: the same HTTP interface, the same request and response shapes, the same error codes, and the same user interface.

The old behaviour, including its quirks, is the specification. A difference visible to a client is allowed only as a named, recorded deviation; anything not named is a defect. Fixing a quirk is a deviation and needs a record, not a quiet improvement.
path: 046. The catalogue keeps its public contract

items.title: Context
items.text:
