items.title: Secrets Management
items.text: The architecture view of secrets in Aurelius Atlas. The practitioner's walkthrough — generating your key, registering it, re-encrypting — is the Contributor Guide's Secrets Management.

items.title: Production
items.text:
The running system receives secrets the way it receives every setting: through the environment the deployment supplies at start-up (configuration management) — the store password is a secret type and never appears in logs. Where those values live (an orchestrator secret store, a KMS) is the deployment arrangement's choice; the system asks for values, not for a vault (ADR 018).

  • Ownership: operational secret handling — rotation, loss, break-glass — has a named owner and a rehearsed path (ADR 028).
  • Pipeline boundaries: CI token and secret handling follows the pipeline's declared scoping; artifacts carry inventories so a leaked dependency is a lookup (ADR 033).
  • TLS material: a deployment serves its own certificates; the repository's material is development-only (TLS Certificates).

items.title: Development and CI
items.text:
Three rules keep developer secrets honest; the commands for each are the contributor guide's.

  • Ciphertext travels with the code (ADR 008): each project's real settings are committed encrypted to a recipient list; plaintext files carry dev defaults only. Ciphertext is the source of truth — an edit that is not re-encrypted is undone by the next CI run.
  • Keys are per person, not shared: each developer holds their own key, and the recipient set is declared in version control. Adding a person is a key-list change; removing one is rotation.
Why keys per person, not one team key?

A shared key has to be replaced whenever anyone leaves — and every encrypted file re-encrypted under the fear of who still has the old copy. With per-person recipients, offboarding is removing one name from the recipient list and rotating: the departure is the rotation, with no secret to hunt down.

  • Decryption is a task dependency: every run that reads configuration first decrypts, so a run either has its configuration before it starts or fails naming the key it needed — the loud failure ADR 018 requires.

A fresh clone fails tests until your key is registered

Almost every serve, test, and e2e target first runs a decrypt step. Decryption only succeeds once your public key is on the recipient list. Until then, commands fail with a decryption error — this is expected, not a broken setup; the contributor guide walks through registering your key.

items.title: Vision & Strategy
items.text:
Why Aurelius Atlas exists, whom it serves, and where it is going. All four pages are written from material that already exists: ADRs 046–052 and the conversion roadmap.

Page Scope Source of content Mission Statement Data governance for the data lake, with Atlas's public contract and one store (ADRs 046, 047) ADRs 046–050 Business Objectives Fidelity to the Atlas contract, a maintainable Python codebase, one-machine operation ADRs 006, 046, 051 Stakeholder Analysis Catalogue operators, data stewards, migrating Atlas users, the maintaining team Roadmap phases 1–6 Architecture Roadmap Link to the conversion roadmap plus the phase themes Conversion index

items.title: Architecture Roadmap
items.text:
The plan of record is the conversion roadmap — increments 0.1 through 6.4, each with a semantics spec, status, and Java origin. This page is the theme-level view: what people can do with the catalogue at each phase.

Phase Theme What becomes possible 0.x Foundations The platform runs: one store, dev infrastructure, the dashboard served, quality harnesses in place 1.x The type system The catalogue's dictionary exists: the vocabulary describing your data assets, its hierarchies, and its built-in models 2.x Entities Assets get catalogued: register data assets, read and update them, retire them cleanly 3.x Relationships and classification Context appears: assets connect to each other, sensitive data is classified, every change is on the audit record 4.x Search People find things themselves: quick search, suggestions, the Atlas query language, saved searches 5.x Semantics Understanding deepens: lineage shows where data comes from, the glossary records business meaning and quality signals 6.x Governance and hardening Governance goes live: sign-in through the corporate identity provider, role-based access, migration of an existing Atlas What must be true before a phase starts?

The phase below it is done: the type system (1.x) is what entities (2.x) reference, entities are what search (4.x) finds, and authentication (6.1) arrives last because the contract is proven anonymous first. Each increment is specified before it is built (ADR 051), so the order is a dependency chain, not a schedule.

Each increment is specified before it is built and lands as one pull request; the roadmap table is the single status record. After increment 6.4, the template's examples leave (DD-019 (the record: apps/aurelius-atlas-server/specs/0-6-dashboards/design.md)).

Why do the template's examples stay until the very end?

They are load-bearing while the plan is being executed: the API and frontend example apps are the demonstrations that the template's wiring (secrets, TLS, CI, serve-with-infra) works for a real app, and the catalogue's own apps ride the same wiring. Removing the proof before the thing it proves is finished would leave the last increments unverifiable — so they leave in one slice, after 6.4.

items.title: Business Objectives
items.text:
What the organisation gets from Aurelius Atlas, the commitment behind each benefit, and how it is measured.

Objective (what the business gets) Commitment Measured by No disruption to the way people work The Atlas 2.4.0 REST API and dashboard behave as the reference does (ADR 046) Parity scenarios per increment, expectations cited from Atlas source (ADR 052) Governance you can afford One store, one service, one dashboard (ADR 047, ADR 050); no Kafka/HBase/Solr assembly to run Dependency and service count stay at the spine; ADR 050's removal map Confidence in every delivery Every increment is specified before built, proven before accepted (ADR 051, ADR 052) Definition of Done in the roadmap; green tests per change Quality you can audit Behaviour lives in executed tests; every rule and function is named by one (ADR 056) The CI suites: unit, parity scenarios, end-to-end; the SonarQube coverage gate Fast, dependable development The whole system runs locally; defects reproduce (ADR 006) One command brings the system and its infrastructure up (ADR 005) What ships is what was tested E2E tests run the built image against real services (ADR 010, ADR 012) The e2e stage: the built image, real services, over TLS Trustworthy supply chain Signed artifacts, SBOMs, verified origins (ADR 029, ADR 033) CI scan and publish pipelines Who measures these?

The pipeline, mostly: every measurement in the right-hand column is an automated artifact — a parity scenario, a trace check, an e2e run, a signed build — produced on the change that claims it, not a survey answered after the fact. The reviewer reads the evidence (ADR 014); the organisation audits the reports, not the promises.

items.title: Mission Statement
items.text:
Aurelius Atlas exists to make data governance of the data lake work the way its users already know — so people can find and trust their data without waiting on IT — on a stack one small team can operate and extend.

The business promise is agility: faster access to information, less dependency on IT, and data assets organisations can act on. The catalogue delivers that as a single source of truth on data assets: where data lives, who is accountable for it, how it moved and changed, and how sensitive it is.

The interface stays business-user-friendly and familiar, so nobody has to relearn it; existing clients, integrations, and muscle memory keep working while the implementation underneath is replaced (ADR 046). Every visible difference is a recorded deviation, never a silent one.

What the fidelity promise does not cover

Fidelity is the REST wire format and the dashboard — the paths a client and a user touch. The Kafka notification stream and hook messages that surrounded Atlas are out of scope (DV-01, ADR 050); integrations that watched the feed poll the API instead.

Keeping that promise affordable is the engineering mission. The system of record is one search store — Elasticsearch 9 — replacing the JanusGraph, HBase and Solr assembly that made self-hosted Atlas hard to run (ADR 047). The system carries only what the catalogue needs: one HTTP service, one dashboard, one store, shared identity, and self-observation (ADR 050).

Why replace the store assembly at all?

Because operating it is the job Atlas made the user take on: a graph database, a column store, and a search index must each be deployed, versioned, tuned, backed up, and kept consistent with the others. Catalogue data answers five verbs — write, read, search, traverse, classify — and ADR 047's argument is that one search store serves all five, so self-hosting becomes running one service and one store.

The standing promise to its users is fidelity: a ported behaviour is accepted only when parity scenarios — expected responses read from the Atlas 2.4.0 source code and its tests (ADR 052) — prove the new system behaves like the old one, and the conversion proceeds in specified, reviewed increments (ADR 051).

items.title: Stakeholder Analysis
items.text:
Whom Aurelius Atlas serves, and what each of them needs the system to be.

Stakeholder Needs Where it is answered Business users Find data and its context in seconds; see who to ask; a familiar, friendly interface Dashboard served at / and /n/ (increment 0.6), search in phase 4 Data stewards and owners Know which assets they are accountable for; classify data and record its quality Classifications in 3.3, glossary in 5.2, roles in 6.2 Compliance and audit Sensitive data identified, access controlled, changes on the record (GDPR and similar rules) Phase 6 (identity provider, authorizer, audit), security tree Analysts and data scientists Lineage and impact analysis; trustworthy, fit-for-purpose data Lineage in 5.1, quality signals in 5.2/5.3 Migrating Atlas users Existing clients and integrations keep working; behaviour differences disclosed ADR 046, deviations, export/import in 6.3 Security and compliance reviewers Identity, authorization, audit trail, encryption with named owners Phase 6, security tree Catalogue operators Run the whole system on one machine; one store to back up; loud failure ADR 006, ADR 047, resilience tree The maintaining team Every rule has a spec and a test; decisions are recorded where made ADR 051, ADR 056, this ledger AI coding agents Nearest-first instructions, specs as the source of behaviour ADR 022, per-project AGENTS.md Why AI coding agents are a stakeholder

The repository is changed routinely by automated agents as well as by people, so they are a real consumer of its documentation: colocated AGENTS.md files give them nearest-first instructions, and the specs give them the source of behaviour to code against (ADR 022). Serving them well is a documentation requirement like serving a new hire well — the same material answers for both.

items.title: How to Contribute
items.text:
Aurelius Atlas is built one reviewed increment at a time (ADR 051). Start with the Development Environment to get a working machine, then the Conversion roadmap to see what is in flight and how an increment runs: spec, code, parity scenarios, traceability, two approvals.

Guide For Development Environment First setup: devcontainer, Docker Hub login, SOPS key, first run Secrets Management The age key, .env/.env.enc, encrypting after edits Operations Ownership Who owns secret handling and incident response, and the written paths (ADRs 028/041/042) Version Control Branches, conventional commits, the two-signature gate (ADR 044) AI-Assisted Development AGENTS.md files, agents as contributors (ADR 022) Documentation Docs tooling, the stub and filling-map convention Writing Style The prose style: short sections, callouts, diagrams; the page pass rules Testing Running the gate locally, test conventions, the covers marker TLS Certificates tls.json, nx certgen, the local CA, cleanup, named relaxations Releasing prerelease/release, the changelog rule, docs publishing Adopting the Template For template forks: the rename and re-founding checklist

Workspace-wide rules for humans and agents live in the root AGENTS.md; every project carries a colocated AGENTS.md and README.md with its own wiring (ADR 003).

items.title: Adopting This Template
items.text:
How this repository adopted the template

Aurelius Atlas was created from the template on 2026-10-09 by increment 0.1 of the conversion (see Conversion). It stays inside the Aurelius Enterprise organisation, so the aurelius identity and the secrets trust root (Case A below) were kept. The Kafka streaming and AWS Lambda slices, the Java libraries and the Gradle build were removed (ADR 050); the repository and docs site were renamed to aurelius-atlas. Sections below that name removed projects describe the template, not this repository.

This repository is a template: a working reference architecture meant to be forked and renamed for your own project. This guide is the checklist for that transition — what to rename, how to re-found the secrets trust, and what to expect on the first run.

Removing example slices instead of renaming

The example applications are designed to be removed as whole slices (for example, the Kafka streaming or AWS Lambda slices). Each project directory documents its own removal steps; see the module map in the repository root for which projects may leave together.

items.title: Rename Checklist
items.text: The template carries the aurelius / aureliusenterprise identity in places that are not generated — they must be edited by hand. Work through this list top to bottom; each item names concrete files.

items.title: 1. Repository identity
items.text: Surface Files to edit Docs site name, URL, repo link mkdocs.yaml (site_name, site_url, repo_url, repo_name, copyright) Clone URL in setup guide docs/contributor-guide/development-environment.md Bot identity in CI .github/workflows/publish-docs-*.yaml, rotate-keys.yaml, unpublish-docs.yaml (info@aureliusenterprise.com) Release verification identity .github/workflows/publish.yaml — the --identity regex hardcodes the repository name Root package names package.json and pyproject.toml (name = "aurelius-aurelius-atlas", author entries)

items.title: 2. Project names and directories
items.text:
Every project under apps/, libs/, connectors/, dev/, docker/, and reports/ carries the aurelius- prefix in its directory name, its project.json name, and its package manifest (package.json / pyproject.toml / Gradle project). Renaming a project means updating all of:

  • The directory itself and every path reference to it.
  • project.json (name, implicitDependencies, dependsOn) — and every other project that references it.
  • Root wiring: pyproject.toml (uv members, dev groups, [tool.uv.sources]), settings.gradle.kts (Java modules), package.json (file: dependencies), tsconfig.base.json (paths).
  • mkdocs.yaml nav entries and docs/api-reference/ page paths.
  • ESLint config prefix values in per-project eslint.config.mjs files.
  • Compose project/network names in dev/**/docker-compose.yaml and apps/*/e2e/docker-compose.yaml.
Check your work with Nx

After renaming, npx nx reset followed by npx nx show projects should list every project without graph errors. A stale reference anywhere breaks the graph immediately.

items.title: 3. Python package names
items.text: Python packages use underscored names derived from the project (aurelius_atlas_server, aurelius_atlas_store_es, aurelius_atlas_trace). Renaming a package means renaming its directory, the name and packages fields in its pyproject.toml, and every import across apps, libs, and e2e/ test modules.

items.title: 4. Java packages and the Avro namespace
items.text:
• Java sources live under com.aureliusenterprise.* (apps/aurelius-java-producer-example/src/..., libs/java/aurelius-java-example/src/...). Rename the package directories, every package statement, the mainClass in build.gradle.kts, and the CMD in apps/aurelius-java-producer-example/Dockerfile.
  • The shared schema lives at schemas/avro/com/aureliusenterprise/example/Entity.avsc; its namespace is the Avro subject (com.aureliusenterprise.example.Entity) seen by every producer and consumer. Changing it is a breaking change for any stream you keep.
  • The subject string is repeated in: apps/aurelius-node-red-example/.env and flows.json, the Lambda handler (apps/aurelius-aws-lambda-example/aurelius_aws_lambda_example/handler.py), the Java producer config (SERIALIZABLE_PACKAGES), the connector config, and every e2e/conftest.py.
flows.json embeds the whole schema

apps/aurelius-node-red-example/flows.json contains the full Avro schema inline (the Kafka node's autoSchema field). Do not hand-edit it; open the flow in the Node-RED editor and re-export after changing the schema or subject.

items.title: 5. Angular library aliases
items.text: The Angular libraries are imported by bare names declared in tsconfig.base.json (aurelius-atlas-ui, aurelius-atlas-data-access, aurelius-atlas-observability) — not under an @scope/. Only @aurelius/atlas-brand (libs/styles/aurelius-atlas-brand, a file: npm dependency used in SCSS as @use "@aurelius/atlas-brand/src/main") is scoped. Rename the aliases, the import statements, the package name fields, and the brand package together.

items.title: 6. Container registry namespace
items.text:
The image namespace ghcr.io/aureliusenterprise is hardcoded in plugin code: tools/plugins/docker.ts (six target definitions). Edit it there, then update the :local image references in the e2e/docker-compose.yaml files and the connector's docker-compose.yaml, plus the org.opencontainers.image.source labels in the Dockerfiles.

All base and infrastructure images are Docker Hardened Images pulled from dhi.io, which requires Docker Hub authentication. In your fork, set the DOCKERHUB_USERNAME and DOCKERHUB_TOKEN repository secrets (the CI workflows pass them to the setup-toolchain action, which logs in to both docker.io and dhi.io); without them every CI job fails at the first image pull. Developers need a docker login on their host too — see Development Environment.

items.title: 7. SonarQube organization
items.text: Each analyzed app has sonar.organization=aureliusenterprise and sonar.projectKey=aurelius-* in its sonar-project.properties. Point these at your SonarCloud organization (or disable the sonar step in CI until your projects exist there).

items.title: 8. Keycloak realm and clients
items.text: The development realm import (dev/keycloak/import/master.json) defines a client with id aurelius. Rename it there and in both consumers: apps/aurelius-atlas-webapp/dev/config.json and apps/aurelius-atlas-webapp/e2e/config/config.json (clientId).

items.title: 9. Documentation references
items.text: After the code renames, sweep the prose: project READMEs, docs/api-reference/, and the design guide all name example projects and the Avro subject. zensical build --strict will catch broken nav, but not stale names in text.

items.title: Re-founding the Secrets Trust
items.text:
Secrets are committed as SOPS-encrypted .env.enc files. They are encrypted for a specific list of age public keys in .sops.yaml — the trust root. A fork inherits the template authors' keys, not yours, so nothing decrypts until you re-found it.

Symptom of an un-founded fork

On a fresh clone, nx test, nx serve, and nx e2e fail with a SOPS/age decryption error. Almost every run target first runs decrypt, which needs a private key matching a public key in .sops.yaml. This is expected on a fork — not a broken setup.

items.title: Case A: Joining the existing organization
items.text: If you are joining the team that owns the repository, follow Registering a new key pair: add your public key to .sops.yaml, open a pull request, and let the key-rotation workflow re-encrypt the files for you.

items.title: Case B: Forking to a new team (no old key available)
items.text:
When the old team's private keys are not (or should no longer be) in play, re-found the trust root by hand:

  1. Generate a key pair for each developer (automatic on first devcontainer start, or via nx keygen).
  2. Replace the entire age: list in .sops.yaml with the new team's public keys.

  3. The old .env.enc files can no longer be decrypted. Recreate the plaintext .env files from the values your team uses (dev defaults are documented in each project's README and settings model), then run the encrypt target for each project to re-encrypt them under the new key list:

    nx encrypt <project-name>

  4. Commit the new .sops.yaml and the re-encrypted .env.enc files together, and confirm a teammate can run nx decrypt <project-name> before merging.

  5. Delete the stale plaintext .env files afterwards — they are gitignored, but leaving them around hides decrypt failures.

Rotate any real values

If any .env.enc file ever held real (non-dev) credentials shared with the old key list, treat those values as exposed to the previous recipients and rotate them.

items.title: First-Run Expectations
items.text:
• The first devcontainer build installs the full pinned toolchain and can take a while; subsequent starts are cached.
  • npm install and uv sync run automatically during container creation; so does age key generation into secrets/keys.txt.
  • Until your key is registered (Case A) or the trust is re-founded (Case B), test and serve targets fail at the decrypt step.
  • Unit tests need only decryption; e2e targets additionally build Docker images and start real services, so they need the container runtime available.

items.title: AI-Assisted Development
items.text:
Automated agents write a routine share of the changes in this repository — alongside bot-authored dependency updates, which have been routine for years. The rule that makes this safe is short: an assistant is a generator, not a signatory. It cannot approve, own, or operate what it wrote, so the gate (the shared set of checks defined in ADR 014) and the human signatures a change needs are exactly the same as if a person had typed every line.

This page describes how we work with assistants under that rule: what counts as done, who signs off, and where the guardrails live. It is written for people reading the system; the machine-facing instructions that agents read are a separate layer, and this page deliberately stands without them.

items.title: The premise: same discipline, faster generator
items.text:
An assistant changes the speed at which code appears, not the obligations that come with it. A change is judged as a change: whoever — or whatever — produced a diff, it passes the same gate, the same review, and the same release rules as any other.

The reasoning behind that rule is recorded in ADR 022; the gate itself is defined once and runs everywhere (ADR 014), and a change answers only for what it caused (ADR 015).

Because the assistant cannot sign, the responsibility for a change rests with the person who asked for it. What that person is agreeing to is defined next.

items.title: The guarantee
items.text:
A merged change always gives the same guarantee, whoever produced it: the gate runs the complete set of checks on every pull request — the commit checks (formatting, lint, types, secret scanning), the unit tests, and the end-to-end tests against real services — and all of it must pass before the change is accepted.

This is the standard both signatures below are given against. It is stated here, before them, so that "I verified it" has a fixed meaning: it means the change meets this guarantee, not that its author liked the prompt.

items.title: Two people sign off
items.text:
Every change carries two human signatures before it merges:

  1. The task owner — the person who triggered the assistant and who can explain the change line by line. Their signature means I understand this and I verified it against the guarantee above. In practice, verifying a generated diff means running the gate locally and reading the diff itself — the prompt is not evidence of anything.
  2. A reviewer — a second pair of eyes, who confirms independent understanding and, in doing so, spreads knowledge of the area beyond its author.

The second signature is not new: the version control guide has always required at least one other team member to review every pull request. What changes when code is generated quickly is how load-bearing that rule becomes. A diff you wrote yourself carries its understanding for free; a diff you prompted into existence does not, and the review is where understanding is either built or silently skipped. The debt from skipping it has a name.

items.title: Cognitive debt
items.text:
Technical debt accrues in the code, and the tests feel it. Cognitive debt accrues in the team: code that works but that nobody but its author understands. It is felt later — at the next review, the next incident, the next handover — and the delay is what makes it debt.

Two habits keep it down, and both predate assistants:

  • The code explains itself. Every project documents itself (ADR 003), and ownership of shared data is a stated answer, never an absence (ADR 042). A reviewer or a new joiner who knows the stack should be able to read this repository without a local dialect.
  • Knowledge spreads through review. The reviewer is chosen to be someone who should learn the area, not merely someone who is free.

Accountability is carried by the team and cannot be offloaded to a single person or an assistant. A team that cannot explain a change it shipped owns a change it does not have.

items.title: Development Environment
items.text:
Follow the steps below to set up your development environment.

This project includes a development container to automatically set up your development environment, including the all tools and dependencies required for local development.

Prerequisites

Docker must be installed on your system to use the development container.

All container images in this repository — application bases as well as the development infrastructure (Elasticsearch, Keycloak, Postgres, observability) — are Docker Hardened Images pulled from the dhi.io registry. Pulling them requires a Docker Hub account: run docker login on your host before starting the development container or running any serve, test, or e2e target, otherwise image pulls fail with an unauthorized error.

If you're using Rancher Desktop, follow the instructions in the Rancher Desktop documentation to prepare your environment for use with the development container.

Use WSL on Windows

If you are using Windows, we strongly recommend cloning the repository into the WSL filesystem instead of the Windows filesystem. This significantly improves I/O performance when running the development container.

items.title: Configure your SSH Key
items.text:
Follow the steps below to configure your SSH key for accessing the repository:

  1. Generate an SSH key.
  2. Add the SSH key to your GitHub account.

items.title: Configure your SSH Agent
items.text: The development container will attempt to pick up your SSH key from your ssh-agent when it starts. Follow the guide on sharing git credentials with the development container to ensure your SSH key is available inside the container.

items.title: Clone the Repository
items.text:
To clone the repository, run the following command:

git clone git@github.com:aureliusenterprise/aurelius-atlas.git

This will clone the repository to your local machine using SSH.

items.title: Environment Setup
items.text:
Prerequisites

The Remote Development Extension Pack for Visual Studio Code must be installed to work with development containers.

To get started, navigate to the folder where you cloned the repository and run:

code .

This will open the current directory in Visual Studio Code.

Once Visual Studio Code is open, you will see a notification at the bottom right corner of the window asking if you want to open the project in a development container. Select Reopen in Container.

Your development environment will now be set up automatically.

What if I don't see the notification?

You can manually open the development container by pressing F1 to open the command pallette. Type >Dev Containers: Reopen in Container and press Enter to select the command.

Detailed Setup Guides

For more details, refer to the setup guide for your IDE:

  • Visual Studio Code
  • PyCharm

items.title: Configure your SOPS Key
items.text: Once your development environment is set up, you need to configure your SOPS key, which is used to encrypt and decrypt the secrets in the repository. Please follow the steps in the Secrets Management guide.

items.title: What Happens on First Start
items.text:
When the development container starts for the first time, it:

  1. Installs the toolchain from the container features.
  2. Installs JavaScript dependencies (npm install) and Python dependencies (uv sync) into the workspace.
  3. Generates a personal SOPS/age key pair into secrets/keys.txt, unless one already exists.

Local TLS material is not prewarmed: every serve or e2e target that needs it first runs that project's certgen target, which issues the certificates it owns into its own gitignored certs/ directory. The local mkcert certificate authority has no workspace home: certgen installs it into the system trust stores on first use (it lives in mkcert's own store, outside the repository) and copies it into each project's certs/; run mkcert -uninstall to drop it entirely — see Data Encryption.

Your first tests may fail until your key is registered

Almost every serve, test, and e2e target first runs a decrypt step to turn the committed .env.enc secret files into plaintext .env files. Decryption only succeeds once your public key is listed in .sops.yaml and the files have been re-encrypted for you (see Registering a new key pair). Until then, commands fail with a SOPS/age decryption error — this is expected, not a broken setup.

Image pulls fail without a Docker Hub login

The serve, test, and e2e targets pull their base and infrastructure images from Docker Hardened Images (dhi.io/*), a registry that requires authentication with Docker Hub credentials. If you have not run docker login with a Docker Hub account, pulls fail with an unauthorized (or rate-limit) error — see the Prerequisites note at the top of this guide.

items.title: Dev Topology
items.text:
The development infrastructure is a set of slices: each slice under dev/ is its own compose project with its own network, named aurelius-atlas-dev-<slice>-network. An app's serve target starts the slices it needs via dependsOn (ADR 005); a slice's services reach each other by service name on a shared network.

The rule that surprises people: services are reached by service name, not localhost. The store's certificate is issued for elasticsearch, so an IP or localhost fails certificate verification, not connectivity. The server's e2e container attaches to the Elasticsearch and observability networks and reaches the store as https://elasticsearch:9200. Certificate plumbing is in TLS Certificates.

Service Host port Slice Notes Atlas server 21000 app Atlas's own port Elasticsearch 127.0.0.1:${ELASTICSEARCH_PORT} → 9200 elasticsearch TLS only; loopback-pinned (CHT-101) Keycloak 8080 / 8443 keycloak 8080 dev convenience; 8443 is the verified TLS path OTel collector 127.0.0.1:4317 / 4318 / 4319 observability OTLP: 4318 browser leg (user JWT), 4317/4319 service leg (shared token); TLS (DD-193), loopback-pinned Prometheus / Loki / Tempo 127.0.0.1:9090 / 3100 / 3200 observability Loopback-pinned (CHT-101); Grafana datasources ride the compose network Grafana 127.0.0.1:3000 observability Loopback only

Each slice documents its own services, images, and run commands in its colocated README: dev/elasticsearch, dev/keycloak, dev/observability.

Keycloak's port 8080 is development-only

The plaintext 8080 listener exists so browser sign-in works in the dev stack; 8443 is the verified TLS path that CI and E2E use. The production arrangement has no plaintext listener — see Data Encryption.

items.title: Runtime Windows
items.text:
Per ADR 031, each runtime the system runs on has one declared window. The pins named here are the answer — this page names where they live, not their values, so there is one place to update. A major-version bump is a reviewed change to every pin at once, approved by the maintainers team.

Runtime Supported window Pins live in Python 3.14 only pyproject.toml (requires-python), .devcontainer python feature, server Dockerfile base image, pyright/ruff target Node.js 24 (LTS jod) .devcontainer node feature, dashboard build.Dockerfile Java 21 (dev tooling for the vendored dashboards' build only) .devcontainer java feature Elasticsearch 9.x (dev image 9.5) dev/elasticsearch/docker-compose.yaml image tag Keycloak 26.x dev/keycloak/docker-compose.yaml image tag PostgreSQL 18 (Keycloak's database only — ADR 047) dev/keycloak compose image tags

Minor and patch releases inside a window follow the dependency rule (ADR 020); the floor rises only when every pin above moves in one change.

items.title: Explore the Workspace
items.text:
The workspace is organized as a monorepo, which means that all the projects are stored in a single repository.

Workspace Structure

The workspace is divided into the following main directories:

  • apps: Contains the main applications and services that make up the workspace.
  • dev: Compose files and configuration for the supporting development infrastructure (Elasticsearch, Keycloak, observability stack).
  • docs: Central location for all project documentation, guides, and reference materials.
  • libs: Shared libraries and utilities used by multiple applications within the monorepo.
  • reports: License and vulnerability report generators.
  • secrets: Your personal SOPS/age key; this folder is excluded from version control.
  • tools: Custom automation (Nx plugins) that wires builds, containers, secrets, and docs into Nx.

Workspace automation is managed using Nx. Each project in the workspace has its own set of configurations and dependencies, allowing for modular development.

Browse the project graph

A great way to start exploring the workspace is to visualize the project graph. You can do this by running the following command in the terminal:

nx graph

This will open a new tab in your browser with an interactive graph of the workspace, showing the dependencies between the projects. You can click on the nodes to see more details about each project.

items.title: Documentation
items.text: The documentation is Markdown under docs/, built by Zensical, checked by markdownlint and Prettier, and published on every merge to main. What good prose looks like is the Writing Style guide; this page is the tooling around it.

items.title: Tools
items.text:
The documentation is built using Zensical, a static site generator built by the creators of Material for MkDocs. It converts Markdown files into a website and reads the existing mkdocs.yaml configuration.

Markdown is a lightweight markup language with plain-text formatting syntax. Refer to the Markdown Guide for more information on how to use Markdown.

The documentation uses the Material design, which is built into Zensical. Please review the Zensical documentation for guidance on how to use its various features.

items.title: Running the Documentation
items.text:
Prerequisites

Ensure you have set up your development environment before running the documentation.

To view the documentation locally, you can use the following command:

nx docs

Open your browser and navigate to http://localhost:8000 to view the documentation. The changes you make to the documentation will be automatically reflected in the browser.

items.title: Adding a New Page
items.text:
To add a new page to the documentation, create a new Markdown file in the docs directory.

Next, update the nav section in the mkdocs.yaml file to include the new page. The nav section defines the structure of the documentation and the order in which the pages are displayed in the navigation bar.

Please ensure that the folder structure in the docs directory matches the structure defined in the nav section.

items.title: Architecture Pages
items.text:
The reference-architecture trees under docs/architecture/ (Vision & Strategy, Data Lifecycle Management, Data Governance, Platform) are written increment by increment: the filling maps on the tree index pages name the increment that writes each page. A page is written in the pull request of the increment that claims it — the facts are fresh there, and the increment's Definition of Done covers it.

A page not yet written is not left empty. It carries the standard marker, so a reader can tell a planned page from a forgotten one:

# Data Storage

!!! INFO "Planned"

    To be written by increment 2.2 (material exists since 0.2 and 1.4), from the increment's
    semantics spec. See the [filling map](index.md) for the page scope and the
    [conversion roadmap](../../conversion/index.md) for increment status.

The rules: the Planned admonition names exactly one increment (or the page's material is already merged, written when convenient), the tree index carries the per-page map, and a page whose increment has merged is written in that same PR — not later. Removing the marker is writing the page.

What an architecture page may say is governed by the litmus test — would this detail still matter if we replaced every technology in the stack? Role-level properties stay; design detail goes to the component's API Reference page (each doubles as its design documentation), a Contributor Guide page, or the slice's README — with a pointer left behind. The rules are on the Writing Style page.

items.title: Architecture Decisions
items.text: Significant technical and organisational decisions are recorded as Architecture Decision Records under docs/architecture/adr/. When a change you are making establishes, alters, or reverses a decision that constrains the project, propose an ADR as part of the pull request using the ADR Template. Keep records business-focused: the reasoning belongs in the ADR, the implementation in the code and project documentation.

items.title: Linting
items.text:
This project is configured to use markdownlint to ensure consistent Markdown styling and formatting across the documentation. The linter is automatically run when you commit changes to the repository.

You can configure the linter rules in the .markdownlint.json file. Refer to the markdownlint rules for more information on the available rules.

Use a Markdown Linter Extension

We recommend installing a Markdown linter extension in your editor to help identify and fix issues as you write. The development container is pre-configured with the markdownlint extension for Visual Studio Code.

items.title: Formatting
items.text:
The documentation is formatted using Prettier, an opinionated code formatter that ensures consistent style across the project. Prettier is automatically run when you save a Markdown file in the editor.

You can configure the formatting rules in the .prettierrc.json file. Refer to the Prettier options for more information on the available options.

items.title: Publishing the Documentation
items.text:
The documentation is published automatically when changes are merged into the main branch. A GitHub Action workflow is trigged to build the documentation and push it to the public-docs branch. The published documentation is hosted on GitHub Pages.

For review purposes, documentation is also published for pull requests. A link to the published documentation is provided as a comment on the pull request. This allows reviewers to view the changes in the documentation before merging the pull request. When the pull request is merged, this documentation is removed.

items.title: Versioning
items.text: This project uses mike (the Zensical-compatible fork) to manage the documentation versions. Versions are defined by tags in the repository, and the documentation for each version is published to a separate directory. The main branch is aliased to the latest directory, which is the default version displayed on the website.

items.title: Operations Ownership
items.text: Two records name an owner and a written path where the system had none: the handling of operational secrets (ADR 028) and the response to a failure of the running system (ADR 041). The owner named by both is the same role, because this is one team.

items.title: The owner
items.text:
The maintainers team — the role whose two signatures carry every change (ADR 044) — answers for:

  • rotation, loss, and break-glass for real secrets and age keys (ADR 028 R1);
  • the response to a failure of the running system, from noticing to closing (ADR 041 R1).

The owner is a role, not a person: when a person leaves, the duties move with the pull request that removes their key from .sops.yaml. This page is the written path both records require (ADR 028 R2–R4, ADR 041 R2); the first rehearsals are scheduled at the bottom.

items.title: Secret handling
items.text:
Storage is decided by ADR 008: .env.enc per project, encrypted with SOPS to the recipient set in .sops.yaml; per-person age keys at secrets/keys.txt, never committed.

  • Adding a person — the rehearsed case, and the easy direction. The person generates a key on first devcontainer start.
  • A reviewed change adds it to .sops.yaml.
  • The key tooling (update-keys, the rotate-keys workflow) re-encrypts every .env.enc for the new set.
  • Urgent rotation — suspected leak, forced expiry. Any one maintainer acts without waiting: rotate the value at its origin, update the project's .env, run nx encrypt <project>, ship under the normal gate with expedited review, and note the old value's exposure window in the commit message.
  • Key loss — the declared answer (ADR 028 R3). Data encrypted to a lost key alone is unrecoverable; there is no personal-key escrow, by design. The person regenerates a key and membership repairs through re-encryption signed by every remaining recipient. The consequence is owned by the team, written here, not discovered in an incident.
  • Break-glass — temporary access (ADR 028 R4). Any maintainer may decrypt and share one value, for a stated reason, to a named recipient. The grant is logged in the project's issue log with the value name, reason, and expiry; the team reviews grants at the dependency-review cadence.

items.title: Incident response
items.text:
The path from first signal to all-clear (ADR 041 R2); the owner is the maintainers team.

  1. Noticing — a symptom appears, or (from increment 6.4) an alert fires (ADR 040). The first person to notice is the recorder, not the decider.
  2. Triage — any maintainer is the decider: confirm impact, choose investigate / mitigate / accept. Mitigation on dev systems needs no permission; a mitigation that touches real data needs a second maintainer.
  3. Act — the decider acts or delegates. The evidence is inside the system (ADR 016): the observability stack (Grafana, Prometheus, Loki, Tempo), the server's logs, the store's health endpoint — reachable without provisioning anything external (ADR 041 R4).
  4. Escalate — possible data loss pulls in the dataset's owner (below); suspected secret exposure switches to the rotation path above.
  5. All-clear and record — the decider declares the end and writes the one-page record: symptoms, actions, cause, follow-ups (ADR 041 R5). Follow-ups that should become triggers become alert rules at 6.4 (ADR 041 R6).

items.title: Dataset Ownership
items.text:
ADR 042 R1/R5/R6: the owner is the workspace project that writes the dataset, named beside it; a new dataset arrives with its owner named in the change that creates it — one line, not a ceremony.

Dataset Owner Elasticsearch: aurelius-atlas-typedefs (entity indices from 2.2, audit from 3.5) aurelius-atlas-server Keycloak realm and its Postgres database dev/keycloak Operational signals (metrics, logs, traces) dev/observability, custodian of a shared store (ADR 042 R2)

The catalogue's store has one writer — the server — so shape arbitration has no live subject in the spine; it applies from the first dataset with a second reader-writer.

items.title: Rehearsals (scheduled)
items.text:
• First rehearsal of the secret paths (rotation, loss, break-glass) on dev secrets in a dev environment — before the first deployment that keeps real data (ADR 028 R2).
  • First game-day of the incident path on the dev stack — same gate, and yearly after (ADR 041 R3); each rehearsal updates this page.

items.title: Releasing
items.text: How to cut, publish, and document a release. The architecture rules — one versioned whole, promoted by a declared path — are Release Management and ADRs 019/024/029; this page is the mechanics.

items.title: The release flow
items.text:
npm run prerelease    # version + changelog + local rc tag; publishes nothing
npm run release       # publish: version, changelog, tag, signed artifacts

The version step is nx release: it reads conventional commits and bumps the workspace as one — the root pyproject.toml version, project versions, and the changelog. A non-conventional commit title poisons the changelog: entries are only as good as the titles, and feat:/fix: drive the version bump.

A non-conventional commit title poisons the changelog

A commit titled "fixes" contributes "fixes". Because the system releases as one versioned whole (ADR 019), a miscategorised title releases a minor where a patch was meant — and the one-version rule makes that number every part's number.

npm run prerelease runs nx release --preid=rc --skip-publish: it versions, writes the changelog, and cuts an rc tag locally, publishing nothing. The tag is for pulling a release candidate and testing it as an artifact; npm run release is the step that publishes and signs (ADR 029).

items.title: What publishing runs
items.text: Per project, docker-build produces the wheel (workspace libraries bundled) and the image; the publish pipeline attaches a CycloneDX SBOM (ADR 033) and the signed artifacts are published so a deployment can promote the validated release along its declared path (ADR 024).

items.title: Publishing the documentation
items.text: The site publishes per tag via mike; main is aliased latest — details in Documentation.

items.title: Secrets Management
items.text: This guide explains how to manage secrets in the project repository. Secrets are sensitive information that should not be shared publicly. This includes API keys, passwords, and other sensitive data. Since we rely on secrets for testing and deployment, it is important to share them securely.

items.title: Getting started
items.text:
The development container includes all the tools you need to manage secrets. We use SOPS to manage secrets in the repository. This tool allows us to encrypt and decrypt configuration files easily.

How do I identify encrypted files?

Encrypted files have the .enc extension. For example, the .env.enc file is an encrypted version of the .env file.

During initial setup of the development container, a unique key pair consisting of a public and a private key is generated for you. It is stored in the secrets/keys.txt file.

I lost my key pair. What should I do?

You can generate a new key pair by running the following command:

nx keygen

Security Warning

Only your public key can be safely shared. Do not share the private key with anyone!

items.title: Registering a new key pair
items.text:
To register a new key pair, extend the .sops.yaml file in the project root directory. Add your public key to the list of age keys. Each key is separated by a comma and a newline.

creation_rules:
    - age: >-
          <KEY1>,
          <KEY2>,
          <KEY3>

Next, create a new branch and commit your changes. After pushing the branch to GitHub, create a pull request to merge the changes into the main branch. Have a team member review and approve the pull request. Once it is merged, a GitHub action rotates the encryption on all encrypted files in the repository to include your public key and pushes the re-encrypted files to main.

graph LR
    K[Add your public key to .sops.yaml] -->|PR| RV[Team review]
    RV -->|approve + merge| RT[Rotation workflow]
    RT -->|re-encrypts all .env.enc| M[main]
    M --> Y[You can decrypt]

Review is the security gate: rotation runs only on main, so a key works only after a human verified it.

Reviewing .sops.yaml changes is the security gate

The rotation workflow holds the key that decrypts every .env.enc in the repository, so it deliberately runs only on main — never on pull requests — and can therefore only re-encrypt to recipients that are already merged. This makes the review of the .sops.yaml diff the single point of control: verify that every added recipient key belongs to a known team member before approving the merge. Never merge a key you cannot attribute to a person.

Ensure a descriptive pull request title

The pull request title should clearly indicate that you are adding a new key pair, and for which user it is intended. This helps in tracking who has access to the secrets in the repository.

Once the pull request is merged, pull the changes to your local repository. You can now decrypt and encrypt secrets using your private key.

items.title: Decrypting Secrets
items.text:
Once the encryption on the files you need to access has been rotated, you can decrypt them using your private key.

Automatic Decryption with Nx

Every project that uses encrypted settings has an Nx target to decrypt the settings. Decryption is run automatically when you run the serve, test, or e2e targets.

If you need to decrypt the settings manually, you can run the following command:

nx decrypt <project-name>

Replace <project-name> with the name of the project you are working on. This will decrypt the .env.enc file and save the contents to a corresponding .env file.

Security Warning

Do not commit your decrypted .env file to version control or share the contents with anyone!

items.title: Encrypting Secrets
items.text:
To encrypt the .env file after making changes, run the following command:

nx encrypt <project-name>

Replace <project-name> with the name of the project you are working on. This will encrypt the .env file for that project and save the contents to a corresponding .env.enc file.

items.title: Testing
items.text: How to run the gate locally and how to write tests that satisfy it. The layer map and what each layer proves is the architecture page Testing Strategy; the gate's rules are ADR 014. This page is the commands and conventions.

items.title: Running the gate locally
items.text:
The same checks CI runs, available before you push:

npx nx test <project> -c ci
npx nx e2e <project> -c ci
npx nx affected -t test e2e -c ci

Always -c ci for test targets — the default is watch mode, which never exits.

Without -c ci, tests run in watch mode and never exit

A bare nx test <project> starts Vitest in watch mode, keeps the process running, and blocks every later step that waits for it. The symptom — a "hung" build that is really an idle watcher — is expected, not a broken setup: add -c ci and it runs to completion with coverage.

The trace tool is a local aid, not a gate: uv run aurelius-atlas-trace check runs collection only, no tests, and prints the functions and rule ids that no test names. CI proves behaviour by running the suites (ADR 056); if you use the check and it finds a gap, fix it by writing the test, not by editing the check.

items.title: Writing tests
items.text:
• Python: test files test__*.py under tests/, functions test__<function_name>_<scenario>. Async tests use pytest-asyncio; fixtures live in conftest.py; pytest-cov collects coverage. Unit tests of store code use the fake client from aurelius_atlas_store_es.testing.fake; containers come from aurelius_atlas_store_es.testing.container.
  • TypeScript: .spec.ts co-located with source (analog pattern), Vitest via @nx/vitest.
  • Test data: created through fixtures, never shared mutable state. TLS material comes from nx certgen (tls.json per project, ephemeral mkcert CA — see TLS Certificates); E2E containers get per-run CAs, and compose health checks gate startup.

items.title: Naming what a test proves
items.text:
@pytest.mark.covers("<dotted.path>", rules=["ENT-07"]) names the function under test and the specification rules it checks. It is a review convention (ADR 056): the marker points a reviewer from a rule id to the test that proves it.

  • Every new public function gets a test that names it — the test is the proof of behaviour; the marker is how a reviewer finds it.
  • Every rule id in an increment's spec gets a test that names it the same way.

items.title: Flaky tests
items.text:
1. Record the recurring failure pattern from CI (the job logs keep the evidence per change).
  2. Find the root cause — timing, isolation, shared environment — before any retry is considered.
  3. Fix the test or the product; do not skip. A test that cannot be made deterministic is removed with a note naming why, not annotated away.

Flaky tests are fixed, never skipped

A skipped test silently deletes the evidence the gate is made of: the run reads as green while the behaviour it stood for goes unproven. Retrying a flaky test hides its root cause — timing, isolation, shared environment — which is the bug worth fixing.

items.title: Pointers
items.text:
• What each layer proves: Testing Strategy
  • Realism rules: ADR 010, ADR 012
  • Parity scenarios: ADR 052, the parity library
  • Per-project commands: each project's AGENTS.md

items.title: TLS Certificates
items.text: How local TLS material is declared, issued, and cleaned up in this repository. The architecture rule it serves — every path TLS with verification, plaintext exceptions named — is Data Encryption; the security record is ADR 039. This page is the practitioner's walkthrough.

items.title: Declare: tls.json
items.text: Each project that serves or consumes TLS owns a tls.json listing the certificates it needs: the service names, keystore formats, and truststores that project's serve and e2e targets consume. The server, the identity provider slice, and the observability slice each declare their own; there is no central certificate manifest.

items.title: Issue: nx certgen
items.text:
npx nx certgen <project>    # issue this project's material into its certs/ directory
  • Material lands in the project's own gitignored certs/: PEM keypairs, PKCS12 keystores, a JVM truststore.p12 where needed, and a ca.pem copy for pure clients.
  • The certificate authority itself has no workspace home: certgen installs mkcert's own root CA into the system trust stores (it lives in mkcert's per-machine store, outside the repository) and copies it into each project's certs/.
Why the CA lives outside the repository

Trust is installed, not cloned: the root CA sits in mkcert's per-machine store, where the operating system's trust machinery finds it. Committing a CA would ship a trust decision; certgen reissues material per machine instead, so a fresh clone becomes trusted by running nx certgen, not by receiving a key.

  • Generation is on demand: serve and e2e targets declare a certgen dependency, which itself depends on decrypt, because truststore passwords live encrypted in each project's .env.enc (see Secrets Management).
  • Service names appear in the certificates, so clients must reach services by the name in the certificate — the compose service name, not localhost (see Development Environment).

Service-name verification fails on localhost

Pointing a client at localhost or an IP address — the reflex from a laptop install — fails certificate verification, not connectivity: the store's certificate is issued for elasticsearch. Join the slice's compose network and use the service name, as the server's e2e container does.

items.title: Clean up
items.text:
npx nx certclean <project>    # remove this project's material, keep the CA
mkcert -uninstall             # drop the CA and its system trust entries entirely

certclean removes a project's material but never the CA, which other projects share.

Nothing in certs/ is production material

Copying a certs/ file into a deployment ships a development key whose CA is every developer's laptop: the deployment serves a certificate no client trusts, and worse, one whose CA is public. A deployment generates its own CA and key material; the repository's exists to make TLS the default locally, not to travel.

items.title: Named development relaxations
items.text:
The architecture page names the rule; these are the specific plaintext exceptions a developer sees, each accepted deliberately (ADR 039):

Why is a plaintext listener a named exception and not a defect?

Because it is a developer convenience on a wire that never leaves the machine (ADR 039's R4), and R1's rule is that such relaxations are written down, not implied. The line R4 guards: the same plaintext path outside the development arrangement — the localhost URL copied into a deployment — is a defect, which is why each occurrence carries a comment naming the record.

  • The identity provider slice serves a plaintext HTTP listener (port 8080) so the developer browser opens a familiar URL; its TLS listener (8443) serves every CI/E2E path.
  • Browser-facing developer surfaces (SPA dev-server, Grafana, Storybook) stay plaintext on a developer machine.
  • Playwright's bundled browsers carry their own trust stores and cannot enroll the mkcert root, so frontend E2E page navigation skips browser certificate verification (ignore_https_errors). The E2E suite verifies the same browser-facing endpoint against the CA out-of-band (hostname + chain), and nginx still verifies the backend with proxy_ssl_verify.
Why does frontend E2E skip browser certificate verification?

The relaxation is the browser's trust store, not the TLS: Playwright's bundled browsers cannot enroll the mkcert root, so page loads set ignore_https_errors while the suite verifies the endpoint's hostname and chain against the CA out-of-band. The encryption and the certificate are both proven — just not by the browser's padlock.

Every plaintext occurrence in this repository carries a comment naming ADR 039.

items.title: Version Control
items.text: Every change arrives on a branch, is titled by the conventional-commit format, and merges only after the gate is green and two humans have signed (ADR 044). This page is the mechanics; the rules behind them are the records.

items.title: Branching
items.text:
Always create a new branch for your changes. Working on main directly makes parallel contributions collide, and the two-signature gate has nothing to guard — a pull request exists only once the work leaves main.

Why should I create a new branch?

Creating a new branch allows you to work on your changes without affecting the main branch. This makes it easier to collaborate with others and keep the codebase clean.

First, pull the latest changes from the main branch:

git pull main

Next, create a new branch with the following command:

git checkout -b "<YOUR_BRANCH_NAME>"

Replace <YOUR_BRANCH_NAME> with a short, descriptive name for your branch. For example, serve-admin-status.

items.title: Commits
items.text:
Commit messages follow the conventional commit format. The format is not decoration: the release tool reads commit titles to write the changelog and decide the version number (ADR 019), so a malformed title is a broken changelog entry.

feat: serve admin status endpoint
fix: keep the status timestamp in epoch milliseconds
chore: update dependencies
docs: update README

Each commit message starts with a type, followed by a colon and a short description of the change. To commit:

git add <FILES>
git commit -m "<YOUR_COMMIT_MESSAGE>"

Replace <FILES> with the files to stage (. stages all), and <YOUR_COMMIT_MESSAGE> with a message in the format above.

Use a Git GUI

If you prefer a graphical interface, you can use a Git GUI tool to stage and commit your changes. For example, VS Code has a built-in Git interface that you can use.

How often should I commit my changes?

It's a good practice to commit your changes often. This allows you to track your progress and revert changes if needed.

items.title: Automated Checks
items.text:
The project includes pre-commit hooks to ensure your code meets the quality standards. These hooks run automatically before each commit. They are the local half of the gate — the same rule set the pipeline runs (ADR 014) — and they perform the following checks:

  • Check JSON, TOML, and YAML files for syntax errors
  • Ensure files end with a newline
  • Trim trailing whitespace
  • Lint and format Python code with Ruff
  • Check for Python type issues with Pyright
  • Format Markdown and JSON files with Prettier
  • Lint Markdown files with markdownlint
  • Scan for secrets with Talisman
What if the pre-commit hooks fail?

If the pre-commit hooks fail, you will need to address the issues before committing your changes. Follow the instructions provided by the pre-commit hooks to identify and fix the issues.

How do I run the pre-commit hooks manually?

Pre-commit hooks can also be run manually using the following command:

uv run pre-commit

The pre-commit hooks are intended to help us keep the codebase maintainable. If there are rules that you believe are too strict, please discuss them with the team.

items.title: Pull Requests
items.text:
Once you have completed your changes, create a pull request: push your branch and open it on GitHub with your branch as the source and main as the base.

Give the pull request a title that summarizes the change and follows the conventional commit format — the title becomes the changelog entry. In the description, provide a brief overview of the changes and any relevant information for reviewers, including the conversion increment the change belongs to and the records it touches (ADR 051).

Pull Request Description

Here's an example of a good pull request description:

# feat: serve admin status endpoint

Ports `AdminResource.getStatus` for increment 0.5.

## Changes

- New `/api/atlas/admin/status` route with the version, metadata
  availability, and timestamp fields
- Parity scenarios citing the Java source and its tests

## Notes

- Scenario expectations read from Atlas 2.4.0 source (ADR 052);
  `timezones` deviation recorded as DV-05
- Verified locally: lint, unit tests, e2e against dev Elasticsearch

items.title: Automated Checks
items.text:
The same hooks that run locally run again on the pull request, together with the unit and end-to-end tests against real services. All of it must pass before the change can merge.

What if the pre-commit hooks fail on the pull request?

If the pre-commit hooks fail on the pull request, you will need to address the issues in your branch and push the changes. The pre-commit hooks will run again automatically.

Please address any issues identified by the pre-commit hooks before requesting a review.

items.title: Code Review
items.text:
Every pull request carries two human signatures before it merges (ADR 044):

  1. The task owner — the person who asked for the change, who can explain it, and who states in the description how far they verified it locally.
  2. One reviewer — a second person who confirms independent understanding. Choose the reviewer partly for who should learn the area, so review doubles as knowledge spread.

A merge button that refuses the merge without the second approval enforces the rule; approving quickly to clear a queue is how a fast queue erodes it.

How do I request a review?

Request a review from a team member by assigning them as a reviewer to your pull request.

An assistant may produce, test, and review a change — and signs nothing (ADR 043).

items.title: Giving Feedback
items.text:
When providing feedback on a pull request, be constructive and specific. Point out areas for improvement and suggest possible solutions. If you have any questions or concerns, don't hesitate to ask the author for clarification.

A code review should focus on the following aspects:

  • Correctness and functionality
  • Code quality and readability
  • Adherence to the project guidelines
Good Code Review Feedback

Here are some examples of good code review feedback:

- Good port — the response shape matches the Java resource. Looks solid overall.
- I noticed a small typo in the docstring. Could you update it to fix the typo?
- The mapping logic is a bit complex. Consider breaking it down into smaller functions for clarity.
- The tests cover most of the rules, but rule ENT-04 has no test naming it. Could you add one?

Always be respectful and considerate when giving feedback. Remember that the goal is to improve the code and help the author grow as a developer.

Be Positive

Don't forget to acknowledge the positive aspects of the contribution as well!

items.title: Writing Style
items.text: The style this documentation is written in, and the rules the page-by-page style pass applies. The reference implementation is the Development Environment guide: short sections that each do one job, callouts for the important and the anticipated, tables for enumerations. Every page aims for that shape.

items.title: The shape of a page
items.text:
1. Lead: one paragraph, two to four sentences. What the page covers and why a reader needs it — in the reader's terms, before any mechanism.
  2. Sections: one job per ##, named for that job. A reader scanning the headings should get the page's outline; a reader opening one section should not need the neighbours.
  3. The point first: every section and paragraph states its conclusion first, then supports it. Build-ups bury the answer.

The size rule: no block of prose longer than about seven lines. When a section grows past it, the content is one of these instead:

  • a list — the block is a set of parallel items
  • a table — the items have two or more attributes each
  • a callout — the content is a warning, prerequisite, example, or anticipated question
  • a subsection — the block contains two jobs
  • a diagram — the block describes a flow between parts

items.title: Callouts
items.text:
Callouts carry what the prose must not: risk, prerequisites, the expected question. Use the type for its meaning, not for colour.

Callout Use for !!! NOTE A prerequisite the reader must have met before the steps work !!! TIP Advice that saves the reader time; the better path, not a requirement !!! WARNING A failure the reader will hit, with the reason and the fix !!! IMPORTANT A rule whose violation damages data, security, or the build ??? QUESTION The question the reader is forming right now ??? INFO Background that rewards the curious and clutters everyone else (collapsible) ??? EXAMPLE A worked example or deep dive

Two habits from the dev-environment guide worth copying everywhere:

  • Name expected failures as expected: "this is expected, not a broken setup."
  • Keep the callout's own text short — it is a paragraph, not a section.
!!! WARNING "Your first tests may fail until your key is registered"

    Almost every `serve`, `test`, and `e2e` target first runs a `decrypt` step. Decryption only
    succeeds once your public key is listed in `.sops.yaml`. Until then, commands fail with a
    SOPS/age decryption error — this is expected, not a broken setup.

items.title: Diagrams
items.text:
A flow that takes a paragraph to describe is usually one diagram and one sentence. Draw when the content is a sequence across parts, a decision, or a lifecycle; keep prose for declarations and enumerations.

Rules: mermaid fenced blocks only; at most about eight nodes; label the edges — a bare arrow states a connection, a labelled arrow states the contract; one sentence after the diagram stating what it proves (never "the following diagram shows…").

graph LR
    P[Pull request] -->|two signatures| M[main]
    M -->|nx release| R[Signed release]
    R -->|promote| D[Deployment]

Merge requires two signatures; the release is the unit a deployment promotes (ADR 024).

items.title: Voice
items.text:
• Present tense, active voice. "The server reads its settings at start-up", not "settings will have been read".
  • Guides address the reader ("run", "open", "your key"); architecture pages state facts about the system ("the server reads", "every path is TLS").
  • Name the thing in guides: "nx certgen issues the certificates", not "a tool generates material". Architecture pages reverse this: parts by role, product names only in the anchor line (see Structure rules).
  • Plain words over compressed epigrams. Say the thing straight: "being up to date is the default", not "the default is currency"; "we chase every update the day it appears", not "every update is chased the day it publishes". A sentence that needs a second reading to decode is rewritten, not kept for its rhythm. Compression is allowed in table cells, never in prose.
  • Define shorthand on first use. "The gate (the shared rule set of checks in ADR 014)", once per page; after that, the short name is fine. Team-internal shorthand — "spine", "slice", "the gate", "the ladder" — is defined where it first appears, per the glossary in Architecture Decisions.
  • No noun-stacking or bumper-sticker clauses. "Age by choice is policy; age by forgetting is drift" becomes "keeping a dependency old on purpose is a recorded decision; getting old by forgetting is drift". If a clause fits on a bumper sticker, expand it.
  • Sentence case headings, proper nouns aside — "The CI gate", "Configure your SOPS key".
  • Cite, don't restate. An ADR, spec, or code path owns the detail; the page links it once. ADR references stay parenthetical at the sentence that needs them.
  • No marketing in technical pages. Benefit framing belongs in the lead; the sections are facts.

items.title: Structure rules
items.text:
• The litmus test decides what an architecture page may say: would this detail still matter if we replaced every technology in the stack? If yes, it is architecture. If no, it is design detail and belongs in the component's own documentation. The same test governs ADRs (Architecture Decisions).
  • Role-first naming on architecture pages: parts appear by role ("the search store", "the identity provider", "the collector"). A page names the current implementation once, as a labelled anchor line — evidence, not contract. Ports, env-var names, file paths, version numbers, and commands do not appear in architecture prose.
  • Where extracted detail goes: component detail (settings, storage layout, protocol mechanics) → that component's API Reference page, which doubles as its design documentation; cross-cutting how-tos (testing commands, certificates, releasing, setup) → a Contributor Guide page; development topology → Dev Topology and the dev/ slice READMEs. Every extraction leaves a pointer sentence behind in the architecture page.
  • Production first on architecture pages: the production arrangement is the subject; the development arrangement appears only as a labelled short section stating rules, pointing to the design documentation and guides for mechanics (example).
  • Page = one increment's material, per the filling maps; unwritten pages carry the Planned marker.
  • Status language is exact: written (0.2), Planned, increment numbers as written. No "soon", no "we plan to" — the increment's status line says it.

items.title: ADRs and the design log
items.text:
The record skeleton is fixed — Decision, Context, Requirements, Alternatives, Tradeoffs, in that order — so records stay comparable (template). The style pass works inside sections, never on the skeleton:

  • Lead every section with its answer: the decision in one sentence, the requirement as a gradeable "must", the tradeoff as what was given up. The bold lead-in names the rule in plain words ("Being up to date is the default."), not in a compressed phrase.
  • Long uniform blocks become numbered requirements, alternative tables, and one-line consequences.
  • Sharp edges stay named, in the Decision section, not discovered in Tradeoffs.
  • Callouts apply as everywhere, inside the sections: ??? QUESTION for the objection a reader forms at that sentence ("why not automate the majors too?"), !!! WARNING for a named decay mode the record accepts. A record earns one or two, not one per paragraph.
  • Diagrams do not go in records; a flow that needs one belongs in the architecture page the record constrains.

items.title: Mechanics
items.text:
Rule Setting Line length 110 (markdownlint MD013); wrap prose at ~100 Formatting Prettier, proseWrap: preserve — run it, don't hand-align tables Links Relative paths; anchors lowercase-hyphen; no link rot (strict) Code Commands in fenced bash blocks; paths and flags in backticks Tables Short cells; long text goes in prose, not a cell

Validate with the three gates, in order:

npx prettier --check "docs/**/*.md" mkdocs.yaml
uv run zensical build --strict
uv run pre-commit run markdownlint --files <changed files>

items.title: User Guide
items.text:
Aurelius Atlas helps your organisation make data-driven decisions:

  • Discover, search, and understand your data — find a data asset and its context in seconds, including who to ask about it.
  • Improve efficiency — see who is accountable for each asset, which systems to connect to for access, and whether the data is fit for purpose.
  • Track data lineage — follow the journey and transformations of your data across systems, and see what a change would affect.
  • Enhance data compliance — classify sensitive information and keep an audit trail of what changed, in line with regulations such as GDPR.
  • Guide data quality efforts — use classifications and impact analysis to prioritise where governance controls pay off.

The Aurelius Atlas open-source release serves the Apache Atlas REST API (/api/atlas/v2/...) and the Apache Atlas dashboard, so those capabilities arrive with the behaviour Atlas users already know. Until the conversion is complete, the Apache Atlas documentation describes the behaviour this system reproduces; every intended difference is listed in Deviations from Apache Atlas.

If you are setting up your machine for the first time, see the Development Environment guide instead.
